listen_text: Section. Russell's Paradox (again). In the part on sets, functions, and relations , we worked with a naïve set theory. But according to a very naïve conception, sets are just the extensions of predicates. This naïve thought would mandate the following principle: Naïve Comprehension. the set of all x such that phi holds of x exists for any formula phi . Tempting as this principle is, it is provably inconsistent. We saw this in the section Russell's Paradox , but the result is so important, and so straightforward, that it's worth repeating. Verbatim. Theorem. Russell's Paradox. There is no set capital R equals the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself End theorem. Proof. If capital R equals the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself exists, then capital R is a member of itself if and only if capital R is not a member of itself , which is a contradiction. End proof. Russell discovered this result in June one thousand nine hundred one. (He did not, though, put the paradox in quite the form we just presented it, since he was considering Frege's set theory, as outlined in Grundgesetze. We will return to this in the section on Frege's Basic Law Five .) Russell wrote to Frege on June sixteen, one thousand nine hundred two, explaining the inconsistency in Frege's system. For the correspondence, and a bit of background, see Jean van Heijenoort (one thousand nine hundred sixty seven), pages one hundred twenty four through one hundred twenty eight . It is worth emphasising that this two-line proof is a result of pure logic. Granted, we implicitly used a (non-logical?) axiom, Extensionality, in our notation the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself ; for the set of all x such that phi holds of x is to be the unique (by Extensionality) set of the phi s, if one exists. But we can avoid even the hint of Extensionality, just by stating the result as follows: there is no set whose members are exactly the non-self-membered sets. And this has nothing much to do with sets. As Russell himself observed, exactly similar reasoning will lead you to conclude: no man shaves exactly the men who do not shave themselves. Or: no pug sniffs exactly the pugs which don't sniff themselves. And so on. Schematically, the shape of the result is just: Displayed expression. it is not the case that there exists an object x such that, for every object z, capital R relates z to x if and only if capital R does not relate z to itself. End displayed expression. And that's just a theorem (scheme) of first-order logic. Consequently, we can't avoid Russell's Paradox just by tinkering with our set theory; it arises before we even get to set theory. If we're going to use (classical) first-order logic, we simply have to accept that there is no set capital R equals the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself . The upshot is this. If you want to accept Naïve Comprehension whilst avoiding inconsistency, you cannot just tinker with the set theory. Instead, you would have to overhaul your logic. Of course, set theories with non-classical logics have been presented. But they are—to say the least—non-standard. The standard approach to Russell's Paradox is to treat it as a straightforward non-existence proof, and then to try to learn how to live with it. That is the approach we will follow. End section.

listen_text: Section. Predicative and Impredicative. The Russell set, capital R , was defined via the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself . Spelled out more fully, capital R would be the set which contains all and only those sets which are not non-self-membered. So in defining capital R , we quantify over the domain which would contain capital R (if it existed). Source anomaly note. Source semantic caveat. The displayed Russell definition selects the sets that are not members of themselves, while this prose says not non self membered. The source wording is retained and the mismatch is not silently corrected. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. This is an impredicative definition. More generally, we might say that a definition is impredicative if and only if it quantifies over a domain which contains the object that is being defined. In the wake of the paradoxes, Whitehead, Russell, Poincaré and Weyl rejected such impredicative definitions as “viciously circular”: Quotation. An analysis of the paradoxes to be avoided shows that they all result from a kind of vicious circle. The vicious circles in question arise from supposing that a collection of objects may contain members which can only be defined by means of the collection as a whole Open bracket. Ellipsis. Paragraph mark. Close bracket. The principle which enables us to avoid illegitimate totalities may be stated as follows: `Whatever involves all of a collection must not be one of the collection'; or, conversely: `If, provided a certain collection had a total, it would have members only definable in terms of that total, then the said collection has no total.' We shall call this the `vicious-circle principle,' because it enables us to avoid the vicious circles involved in the assumption of illegitimate totalities. (Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred ten, page thirty seven) End quotation. If we follow them in rejecting the vicious-circle principle, then we might attempt to replace the disastrous Naïve Comprehension Scheme (of the section Russell's Paradox again ) with something like this: Predicative Comprehension. For every formula phi quantifying only over sets: the set prime the set of all x such that phi holds of x exists. Source anomaly note. Source semantic caveat. The quoted authors use the vicious circle principle to reject impredicative definitions, and the comprehension restriction that follows adopts that response. This sentence instead says rejecting the principle. The source wording is retained and not silently reversed. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. So long as sets prime are not sets, no contradiction will ensue. Unfortunately, Predicative Comprehension is not very comprehensive. After all, it introduces us to new entities, sets prime . So we will have to consider formulas which quantify over sets prime . If they always yield a set prime , then Russell's paradox will arise again, just by considering the set prime of all non-self-membered sets prime . So, pursuing the same thought, we must say that a formula quantifying over sets prime yields a corresponding set double prime . And then we will need sets triple prime , sets quadruple prime , etc. To prevent a rash of primes, it will be easier to think of these as sets subscript zero , sets subscript one , sets subscript two , sets subscript three , sets subscript four , and so on. And this would give us a way into the (simple) theory of types. There are a few obvious objections against such a theory (though it is not obvious that they are overwhelming objections). In brief: the resulting theory is cumbersome to use; it is profligate in postulating different kinds of objects; and it is not clear, in the end, that impredicative definitions are even all that bad. To bring out the last point, consider this remark from Frank Plumpton Ramsey : Quotation. we may refer to a man as the tallest in a group, thus identifying him by means of a totality of which he is himself a member without there being any vicious circle. (Frank Plumpton Ramsey, one thousand nine hundred twenty five) End quotation. Ramsey's point is that “the tallest man in the group” is an impredicative definition; but it is obviously perfectly kosher. One might respond that, in this case, we could pick out the tallest person by predicative means. For example, maybe we could just point at the man in question. The objection against impredicative definitions, then, would clearly need to be limited to entities which can only be picked out impredicatively. But even then, we would need to hear more, about why such “essential impredicativity” would be so bad. Footnote. For more, see Øystein Linnebo (two thousand ten) . End footnote. Admittedly, impredicative definitions are extremely bad news, if we want our definitions to provide us with something like a recipe for creating an object. For, given an impredicative definition, one would genuinely be caught in a vicious circle: to create the impredicatively specified object, one would first need to create all the objects (including the impredicatively specified object), since the impredicatively specified object is specified in terms of all the objects; so one would need to create the impredicatively specified object before one had created it itself. But again, this is only a serious objection against “essentially impredicatively” specified sets, if we think of sets as things that we create. And we (probably) don't. As such—for better or worse—the approach which became common does not involve taking a hard line concerning (im)predicativity. Rather, it involves what is now regarded as the cumulative-iterative approach. In the end, this will allow us to stratify our sets into “stages”—a bit like the predicative approach stratifies entities into sets subscript zero , sets subscript one , sets subscript two , and so on —but we will not postulate any difference in kind between them. End section.

listen_text: Section. The Cumulative-Iterative Approach. Here is a slightly fuller statement of how we will stratify sets into stages: Quotation. Sets are formed in stages. For each stage capital S , there are certain stages which are before capital S . At stage capital S , each collection consisting of sets formed at stages before capital S is formed into a set. There are no sets other than the sets which are formed at stages. (Joseph R. Shoenfield, one thousand nine hundred seventy seven, page three hundred twenty three) End quotation. This is a sketch of the cumulative-iterative conception of set. It will underpin the formal set theory that we present in the part on set theory . Let's explore this in a little more detail. As Shoenfield describes the process, at every stage, we form new sets from the sets which were available to us from earlier stages. So, on Shoenfield's picture, at the initial stage, stage zero , there are no earlier stages, and so a fortiori there are no sets available to us from earlier stages. Footnote. Why should we assume that there is a first stage? See the footnote to Stages are ordered in the section The Story in More Detail . End footnote. So we form only one set: the set with no elements the empty set . At stage one , exactly one set is available to us from earlier stages, so only one new set is the singleton set containing the empty set . At stage two , two sets are available to us from earlier stages, and we form two new sets the singleton set containing the singleton set containing the empty set and the set containing the empty set and the singleton containing the empty set . At stage three , four sets are available to us from earlier stages, so we form twelve new sets and so on. As such, the cumulative-iterative picture of the sets will look a bit like this (with numbers indicating stages): Cumulative iterative hierarchy diagram. The solid outer boundary has a single pointed bottom at stage zero and widens upward. Six horizontal solid boundaries mark stages one through six. The printed labels from bottom to top are zero , then one , then two , then three , then four , then five , and finally six . Dotted extensions continue both sloping sides beyond stage six. No individual set, urelement, membership arrow, or quantity of objects is printed. End diagram. So: why should we embrace this story? One reason is that it is a nice, tractable story. Given the demise of the most obvious story, that is, Naïve Comprehension, we are in want of something nice. But the story is not just nice. We have a good reason to believe that any set theory based on this story will be consistent. Here is why. Given the cumulative-iterative conception of set, we form sets at stages; and their elements must be objects which were available already. So, for any stage capital S , we can form the set Displayed expression. the stage indexed Russell set capital R subscript capital S equals the set of all x such that x is not a member of itself and x was available before stage capital S. End displayed expression. The reasoning involved in proving Russell's Paradox will now establish that capital R subscript capital S itself is not available before stage capital S . And that's not a contradiction. Moreover, if we embrace the cumulative-iterative conception of set, then we shouldn't even have expected to be able to form the Russell set itself. For that would be the set of all non-self-membered sets that “will ever be available”. In short: the fact that we (provably) can't form the Russell set isn't surprising, given the cumulative-iterative story; it's what we would predict. End section.

listen_text: Section. Urelements or Not?. In the next few chapters, we will try to extract axioms from the cumulative-iterative conception of set. But, before going any further, we need to say something more about urelements. The picture of the section The Cumulative Iterative Approach allowed us only to form new sets from old sets. However, we might want to allow that certain non-sets —cows, pigs, grains of sand, or whatever—can be elements of sets. In that case, we would start with certain basic elements, urelements, and then say that at each stage capital S we would form “all possible” sets consisting of urelements or sets formed at stages before capital S (in any combination). The resulting picture would look more like this: Hierarchy with urelements diagram. The solid outer boundary has a flat base at stage zero and widens upward. Six horizontal solid boundaries mark stages one through six. The printed labels from bottom to top are zero , then one , then two , then three , then four , then five , and finally six . Dotted extensions continue both sloping sides beyond stage six. No individual set, urelement, membership arrow, or quantity of objects is printed. End diagram. So now we have a decision to take: Should we allow urelements? Philosophically, it makes sense to include urelements in our theorising. The main reason for this is to make our set theory applicable. To illustrate the point, recall from the chapter The Size of Sets that we say that two sets capital A and capital B have the same size, that is, capital A and capital B are equinumerous , if and only if there is a bijection between them. Now, if the cows in the field and the pigs in the sty both form sets, we can offer a set-theoretical treatment of the claim “there are as many cows as pigs”. But if we ban urelements, so that the cows and the pigs do not form sets, then that set-theoretical treatment will be unavailable. Indeed, we will have no straightforward ability to apply set theory to anything other than sets themselves. (For more reasons to include urelements, see Michael Potter two thousand four, pages six, twenty four, fifty through fifty one .) Mathematically, however, it is quite rare to allow urelements. In part, this is because it is very slightly easier to formulate set theory without urelements. But, occasionally, one finds more interesting justifications for excluding urelement from set theory: Quotation. In accordance with the belief that set theory is the foundation of mathematics, we should be able to capture all of mathematics by just talking about sets, so our variable should not range over objects like cows and pigs. (Kenneth Kunen, one thousand nine hundred eighty, page eight) End quotation. So: a focus on applicability would suggest including urelements; a focus on a reductive foundational goal (reducing mathematics to pure set theory) might suggest excluding them. Mild laziness, too, points in the direction of excluding urelements. We will follow the laziest path. Partly, though, there is a pedagogical justification. Our aim is to introduce you to the elements of set theory that you would need in order to get started on the philosophy of set theory. And most of that philosophical literature discusses set theories formulated without urelements. So this book will, perhaps, be of more use, if it hews fairly closely to that literature. End section.

(For more reasons to include urelements, see Michael Potter two thousand four, pages six, twenty four, fifty through fifty one .) Mathematically, however, it is quite rare to allow urelements. In part, this is because it is very slightly easier to formulate set theory without urelements. But, occasionally, one finds more interesting justifications for excluding urelement from set theory: Quotation. In accordance with the belief that set theory is the foundation of mathematics, we should be able to capture all of mathematics by just talking about sets, so our variable should not range over objects like cows and pigs. Mild laziness, too, points in the direction of excluding urelements. We will follow the laziest path. Partly, though, there is a pedagogical justification. Our aim is to introduce you to the elements of set theory that you would need in order to get started on the philosophy of set theory. listen_text: Section. Appendix: Frege's Basic Law V. In the section Russell's Paradox again , we explained that Russell's formulated his paradox as a problem for the system Frege outlined in his Grundgesetze. Frege's system did not include a direct formulation of Naïve Comprehension. So, in this appendix, we will very briefly explain what Frege's system did include, and how it relates to Naïve Comprehension and how it relates to Russell's Paradox. Frege's system is second-order, and was designed to formulate the notion of an extension of a concept. Footnote. Strictly speaking, Frege attempts to formalize a more general notion: the “value-range” of a function. Extensions of concepts are a special case of the more general notion. See Richard Kimberly Heck (two thousand twelve), pages eight through nine for the details. End footnote. Using notation inspired by Frege, we will write the extension of concept capital F for the extension of the concept capital F . This is a device which takes a predicate, “ capital F ”, and turns it into a (first-order) term, “ the extension of concept capital F ”. Using this device, Frege offered the following definition of membership: Displayed expression. object a is a member of object b is defined to mean that there exists a concept capital G such that b is the extension of G and G applies to a. End displayed expression. roughly: a is a member of b if and only if a falls under a concept whose extension is b . (Note that the quantifier “ there exists a concept capital G ” is second-order.) Frege also maintained the following principle, known as Basic Law V: Displayed expression. the extension of concept capital F equals the extension of concept capital G if and only if, for every object x, F applies to x if and only if G applies to x. End displayed expression. roughly: concepts have identical extensions if and only if they are coextensive. (Again, both “ capital F ” and “ capital G ” are in predicate position.) Now a simple principle connects membership with property-satisfaction: Lemma. in Grundgesetze. for every concept capital F and every object a, a is a member of the extension of F if and only if F applies to a End lemma. Proof. Fix capital F and a . Now object a is a member of the extension of concept capital F if and only if there exists a concept capital G such that the extension of concept capital F equals the extension of concept capital G and G applies to object a (by the definition of membership) if and only if there exists a concept capital G such that for every object x, capital F applies to x if and only if capital G applies to x, and capital G applies to object a (by Basic Law V) if and only if a falls under capital F (by elementary second-order logic). End proof. And this yields Naïve Comprehension almost immediately: Lemma. in Grundgesetze.. for every concept capital F, there exists a set s such that for every object a, a is a member of s if and only if F applies to a End lemma. Proof. Fix capital F ; now the lemma on membership in Frege extensions yields for every object a, a is a member of the extension of concept capital F if and only if capital F applies to a ; so there exists a set s such that for every object a, a is a member of s if and only if concept capital F applies to a by existential generalisation. The result follows since capital F was arbitrary. End proof. Russell's Paradox follows by taking capital F as given by for every object x, concept capital F applies to x if and only if x is not a member of itself . End section. End chapter.

listen_text: Section. The Story in More Detail. In the earlier section on the cumulative iterative approach , we quoted Schoenfield's description of the process of set-formation. We now want to write down a few more principles, to make this story a bit more precise. Here they are: List. Next item.. Stages are key. Every set is formed at some stage. Next item.. Stages are ordered. Stages are ordered: some come before others. Footnote. We will actually assume—tacitly—that the stages are well-ordered. What this amounts to is explained in the chapter on ordinals . This is a substantial assumption. In fact, using a very clever technique due to Dana Scott (one thousand nine hundred seventy four) , this assumption can be avoided and then derived. (This will also explain why we should think that there is an initial stage.) We cannot go into that here; for more, see Tim Button (two thousand twenty one) . End footnote. Next item.. Stages accumulate. For any stage capital S , and for any sets which were formed before stage capital S : a set is formed at stage capital S whose members are exactly those sets. Nothing else is formed at stage capital S . End list. These are informal principles, but we will be able to use them to vindicate several of the axioms of Zermelo's set theory. (We should offer a word of caution. Although we will be presenting some completely standard axioms, with completely standard names, the italicized principles we have just presented have no particular names in the literature. We simply monikers which we hope are helpful.) End section.

listen_text: Section. set theory Z minus : a Milestone. We will revisit Stages hit infinity in the next section. However, with the Axiom of Infinity, we have reached an important milestone. We now have all the axioms required for the theory set theory Z minus . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z minus has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, and all instances of the Separation scheme. End definition. The name stands for Zermelo set theory ( minus something which we will come to later). Zermelo deserves the honour, since he essentially formulated this theory in his one thousand nine hundred eight . Footnote. For interesting comments on the history and technicalities, see Michael Potter (two thousand four), Appendix A . End footnote. This theory is powerful enough to allow us to do an enormous amount of mathematics. In particular, you should look back through the Sets, Functions, and Relations part , and convince yourself that everything we did, naïvely, could be done more formally within set theory Z minus . (Once you have done that for a bit, you might want to skip ahead and read the appendix on closure, comprehension, and intersection .) So, henceforth, and without any further comment, we will take ourselves to be working in set theory Z minus (at least). End section.

listen_text: Section. Selecting our Natural Numbers. In the definition of omega and the natural numbers , we explicitly defined the expression “natural numbers”. How should you understand this stipulation? It is not a metaphysical claim, but just a decision to treat certain sets as the natural numbers. We touched upon reasons for thinking this in the reflections section on relations , the reflections section on arithmetization and the section on Dedekind's argument for an infinite set . But we can make these reasons even more pointed. Our Axiom of Infinity follows John von Neumann (one thousand nine hundred twenty five) . But here is another axiom, which we could have adopted instead: Zermelo's one thousand nine hundred eight Axiom of Infinity. There is a set capital A such that the empty set belongs to capital A and for every x in capital A, the set containing x belongs to capital A . Had we used Zermelo's axiom, instead of our (von Neumann-inspired) Axiom of Infinity, we would equally well have been given a Dedekind infinite set, and so a Dedekind algebra. On Zermelo's approach, the distinguished element of our algebra would again have been the empty set (our surrogate for zero ), but the injection would have been given by the map x maps to the set containing x , rather than x maps to x union the set containing x . The simplest upshot of this is that Zermelo treats two as the set containing the set containing the empty set , whereas we (with von Neumann) treat two as the set with two members: the empty set and the singleton containing the empty set . Why choose one axiom of Infinity rather than the other? The main practical reason is that von Neumann's approach “scales up” to handle transfinite numbers rather well. We will explore this from the chapter on ordinals onwards. However, from the simple perspective of doing arithmetic, both approaches would do equally well. So if someone tells you that the natural numbers are sets, the obvious question is: Which sets are they? This precise question was made famous by Paul Benacerraf (one thousand nine hundred sixty five) . But it is worth emphasising that it is just the most famous example of a phenomenon that we have encountered many times already. The basic point is this. Set theory gives us a way to simulate a bunch of “intuitive” kinds of entities: the reals, rationals, integers, and naturals, yes; but also ordered pairs, functions, and relations. However, set theory never provides us with a unique choice of simulation. There are always alternatives which—straightforwardly—would have served us just as well. End section.

listen_text: Section. Basic Properties of the Ordinals. We observed that the first few ordinals are the natural numbers. The main reason for developing a theory of ordinals is to extend the principle of induction which holds on the natural numbers. We will build up to this via a sequence of elementary results. Lemma. Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal. End lemma. Proof. Let alpha be an ordinal with b belongs to alpha . Since alpha is transitive, b is a subset of alpha . So the membership relation well-orders b as the membership relation well-orders alpha . To see that b is transitive, suppose x belongs to c, and c belongs to b . So c belongs to alpha as b is a subset of alpha . Again, as alpha is transitive, c is a subset of alpha , so that x belongs to alpha . So x, c, and b belong to alpha . But the membership relation well-orders alpha , so that the membership relation is a transitive relation on alpha by the source passage on strictorder . So since x belongs to c, and c belongs to b , we have x belongs to b . Generalising, c is a subset of b End proof. Corollary. alpha equals the set of ordinals beta that belong to alpha , for any ordinal alpha End corollary. Proof. Immediate from the source passage on ordmemberord . End proof. The rough gist of the next two main results, the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy , is that the ordinals themselves are well-ordered by membership: Theorem. Transfinite Induction. For any formula phi of x : Displayed expression. if some alpha satisfies phi, then there is an alpha satisfying phi such that no beta belonging to alpha satisfies phi. End displayed expression. where the displayed quantifiers are implicitly restricted to ordinals. End theorem. Proof. Suppose phi of alpha , for some ordinal alpha . If for every beta in alpha, not phi of beta , then we are done. Otherwise, as alpha is an ordinal, it has some the membership relation -least element which is phi , and this is an ordinal by the source passage on ordmemberord . End proof. Note that we can equally express the source passage on ordinductionschema as the scheme: Displayed expression. if phi holds of every alpha whenever it holds of every beta belonging to alpha, then phi holds of every alpha. End displayed expression. just by taking not phi of alpha in the source passage on ordinductionschema , and then performing elementary logical manipulations. Theorem. Trichotomy. alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta or beta belongs to alpha , for any ordinals alpha and beta . End theorem. Proof. The proof is by double induction, that is, using the source passage on ordinductionschema twice. Say that x is comparable with y if and only if x belongs to y or x equals y or y belongs to x . For induction, suppose that every ordinal in alpha is comparable with every ordinal. For further induction, suppose that alpha is comparable with every ordinal in beta . We will show that alpha is comparable with beta . By induction on beta , it will follow that alpha is comparable with every ordinal; and so by induction on alpha , every ordinal is comparable with every ordinal, as required. It suffices to assume that alpha does not belong to beta and beta does not belong to alpha , and show that alpha equals beta . To show that alpha is a subset of beta , fix gamma belongs to alpha ; this is an ordinal by the source passage on ordmemberord . So by the first induction hypothesis, gamma is comparable with beta . But if either gamma equals beta or beta belongs to gamma then beta belongs to alpha (invoking the fact that alpha is transitive if necessary), contrary to our assumption; so gamma belongs to beta . Generalising, alpha is a subset of beta . Exactly similar reasoning, using the second induction hypothesis, shows that beta is a subset of alpha . So alpha equals beta . End proof. As such, we will sometimes write alpha is less than beta rather than alpha belongs to beta , since the membership relation is behaving as an ordering relation. There are no deep reasons for this, beyond familiarity, and because it is easier to write alpha is less than or equal to beta than alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta . Footnote. We could write alpha bears the underlined membership relation to beta ; but that would be wholly non-standard. End footnote. Here are two quick consequences of our last results, the first of which puts our new notation into action: Corollary. If there exists alpha, phi of alpha , then there exists an alpha satisfying phi such that every beta satisfying phi is greater than or equal to alpha . Moreover, for any ordinals alpha, then beta, then gamma , both alpha does not belong to alpha and if alpha belongs to beta and beta belongs to gamma, then alpha belongs to gamma . End corollary. Proof. Just like the source passage on strictorder . End proof. Exercise. Complete the “exactly similar reasoning” in the proof of the source passage on ordtrichotomy . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Corollary. capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is a transitive set of ordinals. End corollary. Proof. Left-to-right. By the source passage on ordmemberord . Right-to-left. If capital A is a transitive set of ordinals, then the membership relation well-orders capital A by the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy . End proof. Now, we glossed the source passage on ordinductionschema and the source passage on ordtrichotomy as telling us that the membership relation well-orders the ordinals. However, we have to be very cautious about this sort of claim, thanks to the following result: Theorem. Burali-Forti Paradox. There is no set of all the ordinals End theorem. Proof. For reductio, suppose capital O is the set of all ordinals. If alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to capital O , then alpha is an ordinal, by the source passage on ordmemberord , so alpha belongs to capital O . So capital O is transitive, and hence capital O is an ordinal by the source passage on corordtransitiveord . Hence capital O belongs to capital O , contradicting the source passage on ordordered . End proof. This result is named after Cesare Burali-Forti . But, it was Cantor in one thousand eight hundred ninety nine—in a letter to Dedekind—who first saw clearly the contradiction in supposing that there is a set of all the ordinals. As van Heijenoort explains: Quotation. Burali-Forti himself considered the contradiction as establishing, by reductio ad absurdum, the result that the natural ordering of the ordinals is just a partial ordering. Ordinals are sets which are individually well-ordered by membership, and collectively well-ordered by membership (without collectively constituting a set). However, with the addition of Replacement, we have reached another important milestone. We now have all the axioms required for the theory set theory Z F minus . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z F minus has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F minus adds Replacement to set theory Z minus . End definition. This stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory ( minus something which we will come to later). Fraenkel gets the honour, since he is credited with the formulation of Replacement in one thousand nine hundred twenty two , although the first precise formulation was due to Thoralf Skolem (one thousand nine hundred twenty two) . End section.

listen_text: Section. Introduction. Replacement is the axiom scheme which makes the difference between set theory Z F and set theory Z . We helped ourselves to it throughout the source passage on chap and the source passage on chap . In this chapter, we will finally consider the question: is Replacement justified? To make the question sharp, it is worth observing that Replacement is really rather strong. We will get a sense of just how strong it is, during this chapter (and again in the source passage on sec ). But this will suggest that justification really is required. We will discuss two kinds of justification. Roughly: an extrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by its fruits; an intrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by suggesting that it is vindicated by the mathematical concepts in question. We will get a greater sense of what this means during this chapter, but it is just the tip of an iceberg. For more, see in particular Penelope Maddy ( one thousand nine hundred eighty eight and one thousand nine hundred eighty eight ). End section.

listen_text: Section. Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement. We start by considering an extrinsic attempt to justify Replacement. Boolos suggests one, as follows. Quotation. Open bracket. Ellipsis. Close bracket. the reason for adopting the axioms of replacement is quite simple: they have many desirable consequences and (apparently) no undesirable ones. In addition to theorems about the iterative conception, the consequences include a satisfactory if not ideal theory of infinite numbers, and a highly desirable result that justifies inductive definitions on well-founded relations. (George Boolos, one thousand nine hundred seventy one, two hundred twenty nine) End quotation. The gist of Boolos's idea is that we should justify Replacement by its fruits. And the specific fruits he mentions are the things we have discussed in the past few chapters. Replacement allowed us to prove that the von Neumann ordinals were excellent surrogates for the idea of a well-ordering type (this is our “satisfactory if not ideal theory of infinite numbers”). Replacement also allowed us to define the capital V subscript alpha s, establish the notion of rank, and prove the membership relation -Induction (this amounts to our “theorems about the iterative conception”). Finally, Replacement allows us to prove the Transfinite Recursion Theorem (this is the “inductive definitions on well-founded relations”). These are, indeed, desirable consequences. But do these desirable consequences suffice to justify Replacement? No. Or at least, not straightforwardly. Here is a simple problem. Whilst we have stated some desirable consequences of Replacement, we could have obtained many of them via other means. This is not as well known as it ought to be, though, so we should pause to explain the situation. There is a simple theory of sets, Level Theory, or the language of set theory for short. Footnote. The first versions of the language of set theory are offered by Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty five) and Dana Scott (one thousand nine hundred seventy four) ; this was simplified, and given a book-length treatment, by Michael Potter (two thousand four) ; and Tim Button (two thousand twenty one) has recently simplified the language of set theory further. End footnote. the language of set theory apostrophe s axioms are just Extensionality, Separation, and the claim that every set is a subset of some level, where “level” is cunningly defined so that the levels behave like our friends, the capital V subscript alpha s. So set theory Z F proves the language of set theory ; but the language of set theory is much weaker than set theory Z F . In fact, the language of set theory does not give you Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, or Replacement. Let the set theory Z sub r be the result of adding Infinity and Powersets to the language of set theory ; this delivers Pairs too, so, the set theory Z sub r is at least as strong as set theory Z . But, in fact, the set theory Z sub r is strictly stronger than set theory Z , since it adds the claim that every set has a rank (hence my suggestion that we call it the set theory Z sub r ). Indeed, the set theory Z sub r delivers: a perfectly satisfactory theory of ordinals; results which stratify the hierarchy into well-ordered stages; a proof of the membership relation -Induction; and a version of Transfinite Recursion. In short: although Boolos didn't know this, all of the desirable consequences which he mentions could have been arrived at without Replacement; he simply needed to use the set theory Z sub r rather than set theory Z . (Given all of this, why did we follow the conventional route, of teaching you set theory Z F , rather than the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r ? There are two reasons. First: for purely historical reasons, starting with the language of set theory is rather nonstandard; we wanted to equip you to be able to read more standard discussions of set theory. Second: when you are ready to appreciate the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r , you can simply read Michael Potter two thousand four and Tim Button two thousand twenty one .) Of course, since the set theory Z sub r is strictly weaker than set theory Z F , there are results which set theory Z F proves which the set theory Z sub r leaves open. So one could try to justify Replacement on extrinsic grounds by pointing to one of these results. But, once you know how to use the set theory Z sub r , it is quite hard to find many examples of things that are (a) settled by Replacement but not otherwise, and (b) are intuitively true. (For more on this, see Michael Potter two thousand four, section thirteen point two .) The bottom line is this. To provide a compelling extrinsic justification for Replacement, one would need to find a result which cannot be achieved without Replacement. And that's not an easy enterprise. Let's consider a further problem which arises for any attempt to offer a purely extrinsic justification for Replacement. (This problem is perhaps more fundamental than the first.) Boolos does not just point out that Replacement has many desirable consequences. He also states that Replacement has “(apparently) no undesirable” consequences. But this parenthetical caveat, “apparently,” is surely absolutely crucial. Recall how we ended up here: Naïve Comprehension ran into inconsistency, and we responded to this inconsistency by embracing the cumulative-iterative conception of set. This conception comes equipped with a story which, we hope, assures us of its consistency. But if we cannot justify Replacement from within that story, then we have (as yet) no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent. Or rather: we have no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent, apart from the (perhaps merely contingent) fact that no one has discovered a contradiction yet. In exactly that sense, Boolos's comment seems to come down to this: “(apparently) set theory Z F is consistent”. We should demand greater reassurance of consistency than this. This issue will affect any purely extrinsic attempt to justify Replacement, that is, any justification which is couched solely in terms of the (known) consequences of set theory Z F . As such, we will want to look for an intrinsic justification of Replacement, that is, a justification which suggests that the story which we told about sets somehow “already” commits us to Replacement. End section.

But, in fact, the set theory Z sub r is strictly stronger than set theory Z , since it adds the claim that every set has a rank (hence my suggestion that we call it the set theory Z sub r ). Indeed, the set theory Z sub r delivers: a perfectly satisfactory theory of ordinals; results which stratify the hierarchy into well-ordered stages; a proof of the membership relation -Induction; and a version of Transfinite Recursion. In short: although Boolos didn't know this, all of the desirable consequences which he mentions could have been arrived at without Replacement; he simply needed to use the set theory Z sub r rather than set theory Z . (Given all of this, why did we follow the conventional route, of teaching you set theory Z F , rather than the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r ? There are two reasons. First: for purely historical reasons, starting with the language of set theory is rather nonstandard; we wanted to equip you to be able to read more standard discussions of set theory. Second: when you are ready to appreciate the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r , you can simply read Michael Potter two thousand four and Tim Button two thousand twenty one .) Of course, since the set theory Z sub r is strictly weaker than set theory Z F , there are results which set theory Z F proves which the set theory Z sub r leaves open. So one could try to justify Replacement on extrinsic grounds by pointing to one of these results. But, once you know how to use the set theory Z sub r , it is quite hard to find many examples of things that are (a) settled by Replacement but not otherwise, and (b) are intuitively true. (For more on this, see Michael Potter two thousand four, section thirteen point two .) The bottom line is this. To provide a compelling extrinsic justification for Replacement, one would need to find a result which cannot be achieved without Replacement. And that's not an easy enterprise. Let's consider a further problem which arises for any attempt to offer a purely extrinsic justification for Replacement. (This problem is perhaps more fundamental than the first.) Boolos does not just point out that Replacement has many desirable consequences. He also states that Replacement has “(apparently) no undesirable” consequences. But this parenthetical caveat, “apparently,” is surely absolutely crucial. Recall how we ended up here: Naïve Comprehension ran into inconsistency, and we responded to this inconsistency by embracing the cumulative-iterative conception of set. This conception comes equipped with a story which, we hope, assures us of its consistency. But if we cannot justify Replacement from within that story, then we have (as yet) no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent. Or rather: we have no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent, apart from the (perhaps merely contingent) fact that no one has discovered a contradiction yet. In exactly that sense, Boolos's comment seems to come down to this: “(apparently) set theory Z F is consistent”. We should demand greater reassurance of consistency than this. This issue will affect any purely extrinsic attempt to justify Replacement, that is, any justification which is couched solely in terms of the (known) consequences of set theory Z F . As such, we will want to look for an intrinsic justification of Replacement, that is, a justification which suggests that the story which we told about sets somehow “already” commits us to Replacement. End section.

listen_text: Section. Limitation-of-size. Perhaps the most common attempt to offer an “intrinsic” justification of Replacement comes via the following notion: List. Next item.. Limitation of size. Any things form a set, provided that there are not too many of them. End list. This principle will immediately vindicate Replacement. After all, any set formed by Replacement cannot be any larger than any set from which it was formed. Stated precisely: suppose you form a set the image of capital A under tau equals the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A using Replacement; then the image of capital A under tau has cardinality at most that of capital A ; so if the elements of capital A were not too numerous to form a set, their images are not too numerous to form the image of capital A under tau . The obvious difficulty with invoking Limitation of size to justify Replacement is that we have not yet laid down any principle like Limitation of size. Moreover, when we told our story about the cumulative-iterative conception of set in the source passage on chap and the source passage on chap , nothing ever hinted in the direction of Limitation of size. This, indeed, is precisely why Boolos at one point wrote: “Perhaps one may conclude that there are at least two thoughts `behind' set theory” (one thousand nine hundred eighty nine, page nineteen) . On the one hand, the ideas surrounding the cumulative-iterative conception of set are meant to vindicate set theory Z . On the other hand, Limitation of size is meant to vindicate Replacement. But the issue it is not just that we have thus far been silent about Limitation of size. Rather, the issue is that Limitation of size (as just formulated) seems to sit quite badly with the cumulative-iterative notion of set. After all, it mentions nothing about the idea of sets as formed in stages. This is really not much of a surprise, given the history of these “two thoughts” (that is, the cumulative-iterative conception of set, and Limitation of size ). These “two thoughts” ultimately amount to two rather different projects for blocking the set-theoretic paradoxes. The cumulative-iterative notion of set blocks Russell's paradox by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would not be “formed” at any stage. By contrast, Limitation of size is meant to rule out the Russell set, by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would have been too big. Put like this, then, let's be blunt: considered as a reply to the paradoxes, Limitation of size stands in need of much more justification. Consider, for example, this version of Russell's Paradox: no pug sniffs exactly the pugs which don't sniff themselves (see the source passage on sec ). If you ask “why is there no such pug?”, it is not a good answer to be told that such a pug would have to sniff too many pugs. So why would it be a good intuitive explanation, of the non-existence of a Russell set, that it would have to be “too big” to exist? In short, it's forgivable if you are a bit mystified concerning the “intuitive” motivation for Limitation of size. End section.

listen_text: Section. Replacement and “Absolute Infinity”. We will now put Limitation of size behind us, and explore a different family of (intrinsic) attempts to justify Replacement, which do take seriously the idea of the sets as formed in stages. When we first outlined the iterative process, we offered some principles which explained what happens at each stage. These were Stages are key, Stages are ordered, and Stages accumulate. Later, we added some principles which told us something about the number of stages: Stages keep going told us that the process of set-formation never ends, and Stages hit infinity told us that the process goes through an infinite-th stage. It is reasonable to suggest that these two latter principles fall out of some a broader principle, like: List. Next item.. Stages are inexhaustible. There are absolutely infinitely many stages; the hierarchy is as tall as it could possibly be. End list. Obviously this is an informal principle. But even if it is not immediately entailed by the cumulative-iterative conception of set, it certainly seems consonant with it. At the very least, and unlike Limitation of size, it retains the idea that sets are formed stage-by-stage. The hope, now, is to leverage Stages are inexhaustible into a justification of Replacement. So let us see how this might be done. In the source passage on sec , we saw that it is easy to construct a well-ordering which (morally) should be isomorphic to omega plus omega . Otherwise put, we can easily imagine a stage-by-stage iterative process, whose order-type (morally) is omega plus omega . As such, if we have accepted Stages are inexhaustible, then we should surely accept that there is at least an omega plus omega indexed stage of the hierarchy, that is, capital V subscript omega plus omega , for the hierarchy surely could continue thus far. This thought generalizes as follows: for any well-ordering, the process of building the iterative hierarchy should run at least as far as that well-ordering. And we could guarantee this, just by treating the source passage on thm Ordinal Representation as an axiom. This would tell us that any well-ordering is isomorphic to a von Neumann ordinal. Since each von Neumann ordinal will be equal to its own rank, the source passage on thm Ordinal Representation will then tell us that, whenever we can describe a well-ordering in our set theory, the iterative process of set building must outrun that well-ordering. This idea certainly seems like a corollary of Stages are inexhaustible. Unfortunately, if our aim is to extract Replacement from this idea, then we face a simple, technical, barrier: Replacement is strictly stronger than the source passage on thm Ordinal Representation . (This observation is made by Michael Potter (two thousand four), section thirteen point two ; we will prove it in the source passage on sec .) The upshot is that, if we are going to understand Stages are inexhaustible in such a way as to yield Replacement, then it cannot merely say that the hierarchy outruns any well-ordering. It must make a stronger claim than that. To this end, Joseph R. Shoenfield (one thousand nine hundred seventy seven) proposed a very natural strengthening of the idea, as follows: the hierarchy is not cofinal with any set. Footnote. Gödel seems to have proposed a similar thought; see Michael Potter (two thousand four), page two hundred twenty three . For discussion of Gödel and Joseph R. Shoenfield , see Luca Incurvati (two thousand twenty), ninety through ninety five . End footnote. In slightly more detail: if tau is a mapping which sends sets to stages of the hierarchy, the image of any set capital A under tau does not exhaust the hierarchy. Otherwise put (schematically): List. Next item.. Stages are super cofinal. If capital A is a set and tau of x is a stage for every x belongs to capital A , then there is a stage which comes after each tau of x for x belongs to capital A . End list. It is obvious that set theory Z F proves a suitably formalised version of Stages are super cofinal. Conversely, we can informally argue that Stages are super cofinal justifies Replacement. Footnote. It would be harder to prove Replacement using some formalisation of Stages are super cofinal, since set theory Z on its own is not strong enough to define the stages, so it is not clear how one would formalise Stages are super cofinal. One option, though, is to work in some extension of the language of set theory , as discussed in the source passage on sec . End footnote. For suppose for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y . Then for each x belongs to capital A , let sigma of x be the y such that phi of x and y , and let tau of x be the stage at which sigma of x is first formed. By Stages are super cofinal, there is a stage capital V such that for every x in capital A, tau of x belongs to capital V . Now since each tau of x belongs to capital V and sigma of x is a subset of tau of x , by Separation we can obtain the set of y belongs to capital V such that there exists x in capital A, sigma of x equals y, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y . Exercise. Formalize Stages are super cofinal within set theory Z F . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. So Stages are super cofinal vindicates Replacement. And it is at least plausible that Stages are inexhaustible vindicates Stages are super cofinal. For suppose Stages are super cofinal fails. So the hierarchy is cofinal with some set capital A , that is, we have a map tau such that for any stage capital S there is some x belongs to capital A such that capital S belongs to tau of x . In that case, we do have a way to get a handle on the supposed “absolute infinity” of the hierarchy: it is exhausted by the range of tau applied to capital A . And that compromises the thought that the hierarchy is “absolutely infinite”. Contraposing: Stages are inexhaustible entails Stages are super cofinal, which in turn justifies Replacement. This represents a genuinely promising attempt to provide an intrinsic justification for Replacement. But whether it ultimately works, or not, we will have to leave to you to decide. End section.

listen_text: Section. Replacement and Reflection. Our last attempt to justify Replacement, via Stages are inexhaustible, begins with a deep and lovely result: Footnote. A reminder: all formulas can have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. Theorem. Reflection Schema. For any formula phi : Displayed expression. for every ordinal alpha there exists an ordinal beta greater than alpha such that, for all x subscript one through x subscript n in capital V subscript beta, phi holds of those objects if and only if its relativization to capital V subscript beta holds of them. End displayed expression. End theorem. As in the source passage on formularelativization , phi superscript capital V subscript beta is the result of restricting every quantifier in phi to the set capital V subscript beta . So, intuitively, Reflection says this: if phi is true in the entire hierarchy, then phi is true in arbitrarily many initial segments of the hierarchy. Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty one) and Azriel Lévy (one thousand nine hundred sixty) showed that (suitable formulations of) Replacement and Reflection are equivalent, modulo set theory Z , so that adding either gives you set theory Z F . (We prove these results in the source passage on sec .) Given this equivalence, one might hope to justify Reflection and Replacement via Stages are inexhaustible as follows: given Stages are inexhaustible, the hierarchy should be very, very tall; so tall, in fact, that nothing we can say about it is sufficient to bound its height. And we can understand this as the thought that, if any sentence phi is true in the entire hierarchy, then it is true in arbitrarily many initial segments of the hierarchy. And that is just Reflection. Again, this seems like a genuinely promising attempt to provide an intrinsic justification for Replacement. But there is much too much to say about it here. You must now decide for yourself whether it succeeds. Footnote. Though you might like to continue by reading Luca Incurvati (two thousand twenty), ninety five through one hundred . End footnote. End section.

listen_text: Section. Appendix: Finite axiomatizability. We close this chapter by extracting some results from Replacement. The first result is due to Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty one) ; note that it is not a proof within set theory Z F , but a proof about set theory Z F : Theorem. set theory Z F is not finitely axiomatizable. More generally: if the theory of capital T is finite and the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable , then the theory of capital T is inconsistent. (Here, we tacitly restrict ourselves to first-order sentences whose only non-logical primitive is the membership relation , and we write the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable to indicate that the theory of capital T phi is derivable for all phi belongs to set theory Z F .) listen_text: Section. Appendix: Hume's Principle. In the source passage on sec , we described Cantor's Principle. This was: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B if and only if capital A is approximately equal to capital B. Then, This is very similar to what is now called Hume's Principle , which says:. Then, the Frege number of x capital F of x equals the Frege number of x capital G of x if and only if capital F is equivalent to capital G. End display. End displayed expression. where ` capital F is equivalent to capital G ' abbreviates that there are exactly as many capital F s as capital G s, that is, the capital F s can be put into a bijection with the capital G s, that is: Displayed expression. there exists a relation capital R such that three conditions hold. First, whenever capital R relates v to y, capital F holds of v and capital G holds of y. Second, every v satisfying capital F is related by capital R to exactly one y. Third, every y satisfying capital G is related by capital R to exactly one v. End conditions. End displayed expression. But there is a type-difference between Hume's Principle and Cantor's Principle. In the statement of Cantor's Principle, the variables “ capital A ” and “ capital B ” are first-order terms which stand for sets. In the statement of Hume's Principle, “ capital F ”, “ capital G ” and “ capital R ” are not first-order terms; rather, they are in predicate position. (Maybe they stand for properties.) So we might gloss Hume's Principle in English as: the number of capital F s is the number of capital G s if and only if the capital F s are bijective with the capital G s. This is called Hume's Principle, because Hume once wrote this: Quotation. When two numbers are so combined as that the one has always an unit answering to every unit of the other, we pronounce them equal. (David Hume, one thousand seven hundred forty, part three book one section one) End quotation. And Hume's Principle was brought to contemporary mathematico-logical prominence by Gottlob Frege (one thousand eight hundred eighty four), section sixty three , who quoted this passage from Hume, before (in effect) sketching (what we have called) Hume's Principle. You should note the structural similarity between Hume's Principle and Basic Law V. We formulated this in the source passage on sec as follows: Displayed expression. the Frege extension of x capital F of x equals the Frege extension of x capital G of x, iff, for every x, open scope, capital F of x if and only if capital G of x, close scope. End displayed expression. And, at this point, some commentary and comparison might help. There are two ways to take a principle like Hume's Principle or Basic Law V: predicatively or impredicatively (recall the source passage on sec ). On the impredicative reading of Basic Law V, for each capital F , the object the Frege extension of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Basic Law V itself. Similarly, on the impredicative reading of Hume's Principle, for each capital F , the object the Frege number of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Hume's Principle. By contrast, on the predicative understanding, the objects the Frege extension of x capital F of x and the Frege number of x capital F of x would be entities from some different domain. Now, if we read Basic Law V impredicatively, it leads to inconsistency, via Naïve Comprehension (for the details, see the source passage on sec ). Much like Naïve Comprehension, it can be rendered consistent by reading it predicatively. But it probably will not do everything that we wanted it to. Hume's Principle, however, can consistently be read impredicatively. And, read thus, it is quite powerful. To illustrate: consider the predicate “ x is not equal to x ”, which obviously nothing satisfies. Hume's Principle now yields an object the number of x such that x is not equal to x . We might treat this as the number zero . Now, on the impredicative understanding—but only on the impredicative understanding—this entity zero falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ x equals zero ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero . We might treat this as the number one . Moreover, Hume's Principle entails that zero is not equal to one , since there cannot be a bijection from the non-self-identical objects to the objects identical with zero (there are none of the former, but one of the latter). Now, working impredicatively again, one falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ open scope, x equals zero or x equals one, close scope ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero or x equals one . We might treat this as the number two , and we can show that zero is not equal to two and one is not equal to two and so on. In short, taken impredicatively, Hume's Principle entails that there are infinitely many objects. And this has encouraged neo-Fregean logicists to take Hume's Principle as the foundation for arithmetic. Frege himself, though, did not take Hume's Principle as his foundation for arithmetic. Instead, Frege proved Hume's Principle from an explicit definition: the Frege number of x capital F of x is defined as the extension of the concept capital F is equivalent to capital Phi . In modern terms, we might attempt to render this as the Frege number of x capital F of x equals the set of capital G such that capital F is equivalent to capital G ; but this will pull us back into the problems of Naïve Comprehension. End section. End chapter.

listen_text: Section. The Continuum Hypothesis. The previous result hints (correctly) that cardinal exponentiation would be quite easy, if infinite cardinals are guaranteed to “play straightforwardly” with powers of two , that is, (by the lemma on Size Powersettwo Exp ) with taking powersets. But we cannot assume that infinite cardinals do play straightforwardly powersets. To start unpacking this, we introduce some nice notation. Definition. Where the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is the least cardinal strictly greater than the cardinal a , we define two infinite sequences: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. aleph over zero of is defined as omega applied to beth over zero. Then, aleph over alpha ordinal plus one of is defined as the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over alpha, close scope beth over alpha plus one. Then, aleph over alpha of is defined as the union over beta is less than alpha of aleph over beta of beth over alpha. End display. End displayed expression. End definition. The definition of the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is in order, since the lemma on No Largest Cardinal tells us that, for each cardinal the cardinal a , there is some cardinal greater than the cardinal a , and Transfinite Induction guarantees that there is a least cardinal greater than the cardinal a . The rest of the definition of the cardinal a is provided by transfinite recursion. Cantor introduced this “ aleph ” notation; this is aleph, the first letter in the Hebrew alphabet and the first letter in the Hebrew word for “infinite”. Peirce introduced the “ beth ” notation; this is beth, which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabet. Footnote. Peirce used this notation in a letter to Cantor of December one thousand nine hundred. Unfortunately, Peirce also gave a bad argument there that beth subscript alpha does not exist for alpha is greater than or equal to omega . End footnote. Now, these notations provide us with infinite cardinals. Proposition. aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are cardinals, for every ordinal alpha . End proposition. Proof. Both results hold by a simple transfinite induction. aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero is a cardinal by the source passage on omegaisacardinal . Assuming aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are both cardinals, aleph over alpha plus one and beth over alpha plus one are explicitly defined as cardinals. And the union of a set of cardinals is a cardinal, by the source passage on unioncardinalscardinal . End proof. Moreover, every infinite cardinal is an aleph : Proposition. If the cardinal a is an infinite cardinal, then the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma for some unique gamma . End proposition. Proof. By transfinite induction on cardinals. For induction, suppose that if the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a then the cardinal b equals aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b . If the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal b for some the cardinal b , then the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b, close scope . If the cardinal a is not the successor of any cardinal, then since cardinals are ordinals the cardinal a equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of the cardinal b , so the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma where gamma equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of gamma subscript the cardinal b . End proof. Since every infinite cardinal is an aleph , this prompts us to ask: is every infinite cardinal a beth ? Certainly if that were the case, then the infinite cardinals would “play straightforwardly” with the operation of taking powersets. Indeed, we would have the following: Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). aleph subscript alpha of equals beth subscript alpha , for all alpha . Moreover, if GCH held, then we could make some considerable simplifications with cardinal exponentiation. In particular, we could show that when the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a , the value of cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b is trapped by the cardinal a is less than or equal to cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b . We could then go on to give precise conditions which determine which of the two possibilities obtains (that is, whether the cardinal a equals cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b or cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal a ). Footnote. The condition is dictated by cofinality. End footnote. But GCH is a hypothesis, not a theorem. In fact, Kurt Gödel (one thousand nine hundred thirty eight) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent, then so is set theory Z F C plus GCH . But it later turned out that we can equally add negation GCH to set theory Z F C . Indeed, consider the simplest non-trivial instance of GCH, namely: Continuum Hypothesis (CH). aleph subscript one of equals beth subscript one . Paul J. Cohen (one thousand nine hundred sixty three) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent then so is set theory Z F C plus not CH . So the Continuum Hypothesis is independent from set theory Z F C . The Continuum Hypothesis is so-called, since “the continuum” is another name for the real line, the real numbers . the source passage on continuumistwoalephzero tells us that the cardinality of the real numbers equals beth subscript one . So the Continuum Hypothesis states that there is no cardinal between the cardinality of the natural numbers, aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero , and the cardinality of the continuum, beth subscript one . Given the independence of (G)CH from set theory Z F C , what should say about their truth? Well, there is much to say. Indeed, and much fertile recent work in set theory has been directed at investigating these issues. But two very quick points are certainly worth emphasising. First: it does not immediately follow from these formal independence results that either GCH or CH is indeterminate in truth value. After all, maybe we just need to add more axioms, which strike us as natural, and which will settle the question one way or another. Gödel himself suggested that this was the right response. Second: the independence of CH from set theory Z F C is certainly striking, but it is certainly not incredible (in the literal sense). listen_text: Section. The Tarski—Scott Trick. In the source passage on defcardinalasordinal , we defined cardinals as ordinals. To do this, we assumed the Axiom of Well-Ordering. We did this, for no other reason than that it is the “industry standard”. Before we discuss any of the philosophical issues surrounding Well-Ordering, then, it is important to be clear that we can depart from the industry standard, and develop a theory of cardinals without assuming Well-Ordering. We can still employ the definitions of capital A is equinumerous with capital B , capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B , as they appeared in the source passage on chap . We will just need a new notion of cardinal. A naïve thought would be to attempt to define capital A apostrophe s cardinality thus: Displayed expression. the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x. End displayed expression. You might want to compare this with Frege's definition of the number determined by x applied to Fx , sketched at the very end of the source passage on sec . And, for reasons we gestured at there, this definition fails. Any singleton set is equinumerous with the set containing the empty set . But new singleton sets are formed at every successor stage of the hierarchy (just consider the singleton of the previous stage). So the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x does not exist, since it cannot have a rank. To get around this problem, we use a trick due to Tarski and Scott: Footnote. A reminder: all formulas may have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. Definition. Tarski—Scott. For any formula phi of x , let the Tarski Scott set of all x of least possible rank such that phi holds of x, or the empty set if there are none be the set of all x , of least possible rank, such that phi of x (or the empty set , if there are no phi s). End definition. We should check that this definition is legitimate. Working in set theory Z F , the source passage on zfentailsregularity guarantees that the rank of x exists for every x . This is illustrated by the millionaire who bought a pair of socks whenever he bought a pair of boots, and never at any other time, and who had such a passion for buying both that at last he had aleph subscript zero pairs of boots and aleph subscript zero pairs of socks and so on Among boots we can distinguish right and left, and therefore we can make a selection of one out of each pair, namely, we can choose all the right boots or all the left boots; but with socks no such principle of selection suggests itself, and we cannot be sure, unless we assume the multiplicative axiom Open bracket. In short, some form of Choice is needed to prove the following: If you have countably many pairs of socks, then you have (only) countably many socks. The moral is that Countable Choice was used repeatedly, without much awareness of its users. The philosophical question is: How could we justify Countable Choice? An attempt at an intuitive justification might invoke an appeal to a supertask. Suppose we make the first choice in the fraction one over two a minute, our second choice in the fraction one over four a minute, and so on, our n indexed choice in the fraction one over two superscript n a minute, and so on Then within one minute, we will have made an omega -sequence of choices, and defined a choice function. For another, it seems to bind up mathematics in metaphysical possibility. More important: it is not going to give us any justification for Choice tout court, rather than mere Countable Choice. For if we need every set to have a choice function, then we'll need to be able to perform a “supertask of arbitrary ordinal length.” Bluntly, that idea is laughable. End section.
