In one thousand eight hundred seventy eight , Cantor stated that a countable union of countable sets is countable. He did not present a proof, perhaps indicating that he took the proof to be obvious. Now, cautious as we are, we proved a more general version of this result in the source passage on kappaunionkappasize . But our proof explicitly assumed Choice. And even the proof of the less general result requires Countable Choice. Theorem. in set theory Z minus plus Countable Choice . If capital A subscript n is countable for each n belongs to omega , then the union over n is less than omega of capital A subscript n is countable. End theorem. Proof. Without loss of generality, suppose that each capital A subscript n is not equal to the empty set . So for each n belongs to omega there is a surjection f subscript n colon omega maps to capital A subscript n . Define f colon omega times omega maps to the union over n is less than omega of capital A subscript n by f of m and n equals f subscript n of m . The result follows because omega times omega is countable ( the source passage on natsquaredenumerable ) and f is a surjection. End proof. Did you spot the use of the Countable Choice? It is used to choose our sequence of functions f subscript zero , f subscript one , f subscript two , and so on Footnote. A similar use of Choice occurred in the source passage on kappaunionkappasize , when we gave the instruction “For each beta belongs to the cardinal a , fix an injection f subscript beta ”. End footnote. And again, the result fails in the absence of any Choice principle. Specifically, Solomon Feferman and Azriel Levy (one thousand nine hundred sixty three) proved that it is consistent with set theory Z F that a countable union of countable sets has cardinality beth subscript one . But here is a much funnier statement of the point, from Russell: Quotation. This is illustrated by the millionaire who bought a pair of socks whenever he bought a pair of boots, and never at any other time, and who had such a passion for buying both that at last he had aleph subscript zero pairs of boots and aleph subscript zero pairs of socks and so on Among boots we can distinguish right and left, and therefore we can make a selection of one out of each pair, namely, we can choose all the right boots or all the left boots; but with socks no such principle of selection suggests itself, and we cannot be sure, unless we assume the multiplicative axiom Open bracket. That is, in effect Choice. Close bracket., that there is any class consisting of one sock out of each pair. (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred nineteen, page one hundred twenty six) End quotation. In short, some form of Choice is needed to prove the following: If you have countably many pairs of socks, then you have (only) countably many socks. And in fact, without Countable Choice (or something equivalent), a countable union of countable sets can fail to be countable. End example. The moral is that Countable Choice was used repeatedly, without much awareness of its users. The philosophical question is: How could we justify Countable Choice? An attempt at an intuitive justification might invoke an appeal to a supertask. Suppose we make the first choice in the fraction one over two a minute, our second choice in the fraction one over four a minute, and so on, our n indexed choice in the fraction one over two superscript n a minute, and so on Then within one minute, we will have made an omega -sequence of choices, and defined a choice function. But what, really, could such a thought-experiment tell us? For a start, it relies upon taking this idea of “choosing” rather literally. For another, it seems to bind up mathematics in metaphysical possibility. More important: it is not going to give us any justification for Choice tout court, rather than mere Countable Choice. For if we need every set to have a choice function, then we'll need to be able to perform a “supertask of arbitrary ordinal length.” Bluntly, that idea is laughable. End section.

listen_text: Section. Intrinsic Considerations about Choice. The broader question, then, is whether Well-Ordering, or Choice, or indeed the comparability of all sets as regards their size—it doesn't matter which—can be justified. Here is an attempted intrinsic justification. Back in the source passage on sec , we introduced several principles about the hierarchy. One of these is worth restating: List. Next item.. Stages accumulate. For any stage capital S , and for any sets which were formed before stage capital S : a set is formed at stage capital S whose members are exactly those sets. Nothing else is formed at stage capital S . End list. In fact, many authors have suggested that the Axiom of Choice can be justified via (something like) this principle. We will briefly provide a gloss on that approach. We will start with a simple little result, which offers yet another equivalent for Choice: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Choice is equivalent to the following principle. If the elements of capital A are disjoint and non-empty, then there is some capital C such that capital C intersected with x is a singleton for every x belongs to capital A . (We call such a capital C a choice set for capital A .) End theorem. The proof of this result is straightforward, and we leave it as an exercise for the reader. Exercise. Prove the source passage on choiceset . If you struggle, you can find a proof in Michael Potter (two thousand four), pages two hundred forty two through two hundred forty three . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. The essential point is that a choice set for capital A is just the range of a choice function for capital A . So, to justify Choice, we can simply try to justify its equivalent formulation, in terms of the existence of choice sets. And we will now try to do exactly that. Let capital A apostrophe s elements be disjoint and non-empty. By Stages are key (see the source passage on sec ), capital A is formed at some stage capital S . Note that all the elements of the union of capital A are available before stage capital S . Now, by Stages accumulate, for any sets which were formed before capital S , a set is formed whose members are exactly those sets. Otherwise put: every possible collections of earlier-available sets will exist at capital S . But it is certainly possible to select objects which could be formed into a choice set for capital A ; that is just some very specific subset of the union of capital A . So: some such choice set exists, as required. Well, that's a very quick attempt to offer a justification of Choice on intrinsic grounds. But, to pursue this idea further, you should read Potter's ( two thousand four, section fourteen point eight ) neat development of it. End section.

listen_text: Section. The Banach—Tarski Paradox. We might also attempt to justify Choice, as Boolos attempted to justify Replacement, by appealing to extrinsic considerations (see the source passage on sec ). After all, adopting Choice has many desirable consequences: the ability to compare every cardinal; the ability to well-order every set; the ability to treat cardinals as a particular kind of ordinal; etc. Sometimes, however, it is claimed that Choice has undesirable consequences. Mostly, this is due to a result by Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski (one thousand nine hundred twenty four) . Theorem. Banach—Tarski Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any ball can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that ball. End theorem. At first glance, this is a bit amazing. Clearly the two balls have twice the volume of the original ball. But rigid motions—rotation and transportation—do not change volume. So it looks as if Banach—Tarski allows us to magick new matter into existence. It gets worse. Footnote. See Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), Theorem three point one two . End footnote. Similar reasoning shows that a pea can be cut into finitely many pieces, which can then be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form an entity the shape and size of Big Ben. None of this, however, holds in set theory Z F on its own. Footnote. Though Banach—Tarski can be proved with principles which are strictly weaker than Choice; see Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), three hundred three . End footnote. So we face a decision: reject Choice, or learn to live with the “paradox”. We're going to suggest that we should learn to live with the “paradox”. Indeed, we don't think it's much of a paradox at all. In particular, we don't see why it is any more or less paradoxical than any of the following results: Footnote. Michael Potter (two thousand four), two hundred seventy six through two hundred seventy seven , Tom Weston (two thousand three), sixteen , Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), thirty one, three hundred eight through three hundred nine , make similar points, using other examples. End footnote. List. Next item. There are as many points in the interval open scope, zero, then one, close scope as in the real numbers . Proof: consider the tangent of pi times the quantity r minus one half; the source formula contains one extra closing parenthesis . Next item. There are as many points in a line as in a square. See the source passage on sec and the source passage on sec . Next item. There are space-filling curves. See the source passage on sec and the source passage on sec . End list. None of these three results require Choice. Indeed, we now just regard them as surprising, lovely, bits of mathematics. Maybe we should adopt the same attitude to the Banach—Tarski Paradox. In fact, Raphael Robinson (one thousand nine hundred forty seven) proved that the decomposition can be achieved with five pieces (but no fewer). Unfortunately, that would require much more algebra than we can present here. However, we can offer some quick remarks which might shed some insight on the proof of Banach-Tarski, Footnote. For a much fuller treatment, see Tom Weston (two thousand three) or Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen) . End footnote. by focussing on the following result: Theorem. Vitali's Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any circle can be decomposed into countably many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that circle. End theorem. Vitali's Paradox is much easier to prove than the Banach—Tarski Paradox. We have called it “Vitali's Paradox”, since it follows from Vitali's one thousand nine hundred five construction of an unmeasurable set. But the set-theoretic aspects of the proof of Vitali's Paradox and the Banach-Tarski Paradox are very similar. The essential difference between the results is just that Banach-Tarski considers a finite decomposition, whereas Vitali's Paradox considers a countably infinite decomposition. As Tom Weston (two thousand three) puts it, Vitali's Paradox “is certainly not nearly as striking as the Banach—Tarski paradox, but it does illustrate that geometric paradoxes can happen even in `simple' situations.” Vitali's Paradox concerns a two-dimensional figure, a circle. listen_text: Section. Georg Cantor. An early biography of Georg Cantor ( gay -org kahn -tor) claimed that he was born and found on a ship that was sailing for Saint Petersburg, Russia, and that his parents were unknown. This, however, is not true; although he was born in Saint Petersburg in one thousand eight hundred forty five. Cantor received his doctorate in mathematics at the University of Berlin in one thousand eight hundred sixty seven. He is known for his work in set theory, and is credited with founding set theory as a distinctive research discipline. He was the first to prove that there are infinite sets of different sizes. His theories, and especially his theory of infinities, caused much debate among mathematicians at the time, and his work was controversial. Cantor's religious beliefs and his mathematical work were inextricably tied; he even claimed that the theory of transfinite numbers had been communicated to him directly by God. In later life, Cantor suffered from mental illness. Beginning in one thousand eight hundred ninety four, and more frequently towards his later years, Cantor was hospitalized. The heavy criticism of his work, including a falling out with the mathematician Leopold Kronecker, led to depression and a lack of interest in mathematics. During depressive episodes, Cantor would turn to philosophy and literature, and even published a theory that Francis Bacon was the author of Shakespeare's plays. text: Section. Georg Cantor. An early biography of Georg Cantor ( gay -org kahn -tor) claimed that he was born and found on a ship that was sailing for Saint Petersburg, Russia, and that his parents were unknown. This, however, is not true; although he was born in Saint Petersburg in one thousand eight hundred forty five. Cantor received his doctorate in mathematics at the University of Berlin in one thousand eight hundred sixty seven. He is known for his work in set theory, and is credited with founding set theory as a distinctive research discipline. He was the first to prove that there are infinite sets of different sizes. His theories, and especially his theory of infinities, caused much debate among mathematicians at the time, and his work was controversial. Cantor's religious beliefs and his mathematical work were inextricably tied; he even claimed that the theory of transfinite numbers had been communicated to him directly by God. In later life, Cantor suffered from mental illness. Beginning in one thousand eight hundred ninety four, and more frequently towards his later years, Cantor was hospitalized. The heavy criticism of his work, including a falling out with the mathematician Leopold Kronecker, led to depression and a lack of interest in mathematics. During depressive episodes, Cantor would turn to philosophy and literature, and even published a theory that Francis Bacon was the author of Shakespeare's plays. Cantor died on January six, one thousand nine hundred eighteen, in a sanatorium in Halle. Further reading. For full biographies of Cantor, see Joseph Dauben (one thousand nine hundred ninety) and Ivor Grattan-Guinness (one thousand nine hundred seventy one) . Cantor's radical views are also described in the BBC Radio four program A Brief History of Mathematics (Marcus du Sautoy, two thousand fourteen) . listen_text: Section. Alonzo Church. Alonzo Church was born in Washington, DC on June fourteen, one thousand nine hundred three. In early childhood, an air gun incident left Church blind in one eye. He finished preparatory school in Connecticut in one thousand nine hundred twenty and began his university education at Princeton that same year. He completed his doctoral studies in one thousand nine hundred twenty seven. After a couple years abroad, Church returned to Princeton. Church was known to be exceedingly polite and careful. His blackboard writing was immaculate, and he would preserve important papers by carefully covering them in Duco cement (a clear glue). Outside of his academic pursuits, he enjoyed reading science fiction magazines and was not afraid to write to the editors if he spotted any inaccuracies in the writing. Church's academic achievements were great. Together with his students Stephen Kleene and Barkley Rosser, he developed a theory of effective calculability, the lambda calculus, independently of Alan Turing's development of the Turing machine. The two definitions of computability are equivalent, and give rise to what is now known as the Church—Turing Thesis, that a function of the natural numbers is effectively computable if and only if it is computable via Turing machine (or lambda calculus). He also proved what is now known as Church's Theorem: The decision problem for the validity of first-order formulas is unsolvable. Church continued his work into old age. In one thousand nine hundred sixty seven he left Princeton for UCLA, where he was professor until his retirement in one thousand nine hundred ninety. Church passed away on August one, one thousand nine hundred ninety five at the age of ninety two. Further reading. For a brief biography of Church, see Herbert B. Enderton (two thousand nineteen) . Church's original writings on the lambda calculus and the Entscheidungsproblem (Church's Thesis) are Alonzo Church (one thousand nine hundred thirty six) and Alonzo Church (one thousand nine hundred thirty six) . William Aspray (one thousand nine hundred eighty four) records an interview with Church about the Princeton mathematics community in the nineteen thirties. Church wrote a series of book reviews of the Journal of Symbolic Logic from one thousand nine hundred thirty six until one thousand nine hundred seventy nine. They are all archived on John MacFarlane's website (John MacFarlane, two thousand fifteen) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Gerhard Gentzen. Gerhard Gentzen is known primarily as the creator of structural proof theory, and specifically the creation of the natural deduction and sequent calculus derivation systems. He was born on November twenty four, one thousand nine hundred nine in Greifswald, Germany. Gerhard was homeschooled for three years before attending preparatory school, where he was behind most of his classmates in terms of education. Despite this, he was a brilliant student and showed a strong aptitude for mathematics. His interests were varied, and he, for instance, also write poems for his mother and plays for the school theatre. Gentzen began his university studies at the University of Greifswald, but moved around to Goettingen, Munich, and Berlin. He received his doctorate in one thousand nine hundred thirty three from the University of Goettingen under Hermann Weyl. (Paul Bernays supervised most of his work, but was dismissed from the university by the Nazis.) In one thousand nine hundred thirty four, Gentzen began work as an assistant to David Hilbert. That same year he developed the sequent calculus and natural deduction derivation systems, in his papers Untersuchungen ueber das logische Schließen I—II Translation. Investigations Into Logical Deduction, parts one and two. End translation.. He proved the consistency of the Peano axioms in one thousand nine hundred thirty six. Gentzen's relationship with the Nazis is complicated. At the same time his mentor Bernays was forced to leave Germany, Gentzen joined the university branch of the SA, the Nazi paramilitary organization. Like many Germans, he was a member of the Nazi party. During the war, he served as a telecommunications officer for the air intelligence unit. However, in one thousand nine hundred forty two he was released from duty due to a nervous breakdown. It is unclear whether or not Gentzen's loyalties lay with the Nazi party, or whether he joined the party in order to ensure academic success. In one thousand nine hundred forty three, Gentzen was offered an academic position at the Mathematical Institute of the German University of Prague, which he accepted. However, in one thousand nine hundred forty five the citizens of Prague revolted against German occupation. Soviet forces arrived in the city and arrested all the professors at the university. Because of his membership in Nazi organizations, Gentzen was taken to a forced labour camp. He died of malnutrition while in his cell on August four, one thousand nine hundred forty five at the age of thirty five. Further reading. For a full biography of Gentzen, see Eckart Menzler-Trott (two thousand seven) . An interesting read about mathematicians under Nazi rule, which gives a brief note about Gentzen's life, is given by Sanford L. Segal (two thousand fourteen) . Gentzen's papers on logical deduction are available in the original german (Gerhard Gentzen, one thousand nine hundred thirty five) and (Gerhard Gentzen, one thousand nine hundred thirty five) . English translations of Gentzen's papers have been collected in a single volume by Manfred E. Szabo (one thousand nine hundred sixty nine) , which also includes a biographical sketch. End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Kurt Goedel. Kurt Goedel ( ger -dle) was born on April twenty eight, one thousand nine hundred six in Bruenn in the Austro-Hungarian empire (now Brno in the Czech Republic). Due to his inquisitive and bright nature, young Kurtele was often called “Der kleine Herr Warum” (Little Mr. Why) by his family. He excelled in academics from primary school onward, where he got less than the highest grade only in mathematics. Goedel was often absent from school due to poor health and was exempt from physical education. He was diagnosed with rheumatic fever during his childhood. Throughout his life, he believed this permanently affected his heart despite medical assessment saying otherwise. Goedel began studying at the University of Vienna in one thousand nine hundred twenty four and completed his doctoral studies in one thousand nine hundred twenty nine. He first intended to study physics, but his interests soon moved to mathematics and especially logic, in part due to the influence of the philosopher Rudolf Carnap. His dissertation, written under the supervision of Hans Hahn, proved the completeness theorem of first-order predicate logic with identity (Kurt Gödel, one thousand nine hundred twenty nine) . Only a year later, he obtained his most famous results—the first and second incompleteness theorems (published in Kurt Gödel one thousand nine hundred thirty one ). During his time in Vienna, Goedel was heavily involved with the Vienna Circle, a group of scientifically-minded philosophers that included Carnap, whose work was especially influenced by Goedel's results. In one thousand nine hundred thirty eight, Goedel married Adele Nimbursky. His parents were not pleased: not only was she six years older than him and already divorced, but she worked as a dancer in a nightclub. Social pressures did not affect Goedel, however, and they remained happily married until his death. After Nazi Germany annexed Austria in one thousand nine hundred thirty eight, Goedel and Adele emigrated to the United States, where he took up a position at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. Despite his introversion and eccentric nature, Goedel's time at Princeton was collaborative and fruitful. He published essays in set theory, philosophy and physics. Notably, he struck up a particularly strong friendship with his colleague at the IAS, Albert Einstein. In his later years, Goedel's mental health deteriorated. His wife's hospitalization in one thousand nine hundred seventy seven meant she was no longer able to cook his meals for him. Having suffered from mental health issues throughout his life, he succumbed to paranoia. Deathly afraid of being poisoned, Goedel refused to eat. He died of starvation on January fourteen, one thousand nine hundred seventy eight, in Princeton. Further reading. For a complete biography of Goedel's life is available, see John Dawson, Jr. (one thousand nine hundred ninety seven) . For further biographical pieces, as well as essays about Goedel's contributions to logic and philosophy, see Hao Wang (one thousand nine hundred ninety) , Matthias Baaz and Christos H. Papadimitriou and Hilary W. Putnam and Dana S. Scott and Charles L. Harper Jr. (two thousand eleven) , Gaisi Takeuti and Nicholas Passell and Mariko Yasugi (two thousand three) , and Karl Sigmund and John Dawson and Kurt Mühlberger and Hans Magnus Enzensberger and Juliette Kennedy (two thousand seven) . Goedel's PhD thesis is available in the original German (Kurt Gödel, one thousand nine hundred twenty nine) . The original text of the incompleteness theorems is (Kurt Gödel, one thousand nine hundred thirty one) . All of Goedel's published and unpublished writings, as well as a selection of correspondence, are available in English in his Collected Papers Solomon Feferman and John W. Dawson Jr. and Stephen C. Kleene and Gregory H. Moore and Robert M. Solovay and Jean van Heijenoort (one thousand nine hundred eighty six) and Solomon Feferman and John W. Dawson Jr. and Stephen C. Kleene and Gregory H. Moore and Robert M. Solovay and Jean van Heijenoort (one thousand nine hundred ninety) . For a detailed treatment of Goedel's incompleteness theorems, see Peter Smith (two thousand thirteen) . For an informal, philosophical discussion of Goedel's theorems, see Mark Linsenmayer's podcast (Mark Linsenmayer, two thousand fourteen) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Emmy Noether. Emmy Noether ( ner -ter) was born in Erlangen, Germany, on March twenty three, one thousand eight hundred eighty two, to an upper-middle class scholarly family. Hailed as the “mother of modern algebra,” Noether made groundbreaking contributions to both mathematics and physics, despite significant barriers to women's education. In Germany at the time, young girls were meant to be educated in arts and were not allowed to attend college preparatory schools. However, after auditing classes at the Universities of Goettingen and Erlangen (where her father was professor of mathematics), Noether was eventually able to enroll as a student at Erlangen in one thousand nine hundred four, when their policy was updated to allow female students. She received her doctorate in mathematics in one thousand nine hundred seven. Despite her qualifications, Noether experienced much resistance during her career. From one thousand nine hundred eight to one thousand nine hundred fifteen, she taught at Erlangen without pay. During this time, she caught the attention of David Hilbert, one of the world's foremost mathematicians of the time, who invited her to Goettingen. However, women were prohibited from obtaining professorships, and she was only able to lecture under Hilbert's name, again without pay. During this time she proved what is now known as Noether's theorem, which is still used in theoretical physics today. Noether was finally granted the right to teach in one thousand nine hundred nineteen. Hilbert's response to continued resistance of his university colleagues reportedly was: “Gentlemen, the faculty senate is not a bathhouse.” In the later nineteen twenties, she concentrated on work in abstract algebra, and her contributions revolutionized the field. In her proofs she often made use of the so-called ascending chain condition, which states that there is no infinite strictly increasing chain of certain sets. For instance, certain algebraic structures now known as Noetherian rings have the property that there are no infinite sequences of ideals I sub one is properly contained in I sub two, which is properly contained in the next ideal, and so on . The condition can be generalized to any partial order (in algebra, it concerns the special case of ideals ordered by the subset relation), and we can also consider the dual descending chain condition, where every strictly de creasing sequence in a partial order eventually ends. If a partial order satisfies the descending chain condition, it is possible to use induction along this order in a similar way in which we can use induction along the less than order on the natural numbers . Such orders are called well-founded or Noetherian, and the corresponding proof principle Noetherian induction. Noether was Jewish, and when the Nazis came to power in one thousand nine hundred thirty three, she was dismissed from her position. Luckily, Noether was able to emigrate to the United States for a temporary position at Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. During her time there she also lectured at Princeton, although she found the university to be unwelcoming to women (Auguste Dick, one thousand nine hundred eighty one, eighty one) . In one thousand nine hundred thirty five, Noether underwent an operation to remove a uterine tumour. She died from an infection as a result of the surgery, and was buried at Bryn Mawr. Further reading. For a biography of Noether, see Auguste Dick (one thousand nine hundred eighty one) . The Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics has their lectures on Noether's life and influence available online (Perimeter Institute, two thousand fifteen) . If you're tired of reading, Stuff You Missed in History Class has a podcast on Noether's life and influence (Holly Frey and Tracy V. Wilson, two thousand fifteen) . The collected works of Noether are available in the original German (Nathan Jacobson, one thousand nine hundred eighty three) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Rozsa Peter. Rozsa Peter was born Rosza Politzer, in Budapest, Hungary, on February seventeen, one thousand nine hundred five. She is best known for her work on recursive functions, which was essential for the creation of the field of recursion theory. Peter was raised during harsh political times—WWI raged when she was a teenager—but was able to attend the affluent Maria Terezia Girls' School in Budapest, from where she graduated in one thousand nine hundred twenty two. She then studied at Pazmany Peter University (later renamed Lorand Eoetvoes University) in Budapest. She began studying chemistry at the insistence of her father, but later switched to mathematics, and graduated in one thousand nine hundred twenty seven. Although she had the credentials to teach high school mathematics, the economic situation at the time was dire as the Great Depression affected the world economy. During this time, Peter took odd jobs as a tutor and private teacher of mathematics. She eventually returned to university to take up graduate studies in mathematics. She had originally planned to work in number theory, but after finding out that her results had already been proven, she almost gave up on mathematics altogether. She was encouraged to work on Goedel's incompleteness theorems, and unknowingly proved several of his results in different ways. This restored her confidence, and Peter went on to write her first papers on recursion theory, inspired by David Hilbert's foundational program. She received her PhD in one thousand nine hundred thirty five, and in one thousand nine hundred thirty seven she became an editor for the Journal of Symbolic Logic. Peter's early papers are widely credited as founding contributions to the field of recursive function theory. In Rózsa Péter (one thousand nine hundred thirty fivea) , she investigated the relationship between different kinds of recursion. In Rózsa Péter (one thousand nine hundred thirty fiveb) , she showed that a certain recursively defined function is not primitive recursive. This simplified an earlier result due to Wilhelm Ackermann. Peter's simplified function is what's now often called the Ackermann function—and sometimes, more properly, the Ackermann—Peter function. She wrote the first book on recursive function theory (Rózsa Péter, one thousand nine hundred fifty one) . Despite the importance and influence of her work, Peter did not obtain a full-time teaching position until one thousand nine hundred forty five. During the Nazi occupation of Hungary during World War II, Peter was not allowed to teach due to anti-Semitic laws. In one thousand nine hundred forty four the government created a Jewish ghetto in Budapest; the ghetto was cut off from the rest of the city and attended by armed guards. Peter was forced to live in the ghetto until one thousand nine hundred forty five when it was liberated. She then went on to teach at the Budapest Teachers Training College, and from one thousand nine hundred fifty five onward at Eoetvoes Lorand University. text: Section. Rozsa Peter. Rozsa Peter was born Rosza Politzer, in Budapest, Hungary, on February seventeen, one thousand nine hundred five. She is best known for her work on recursive functions, which was essential for the creation of the field of recursion theory. Peter was raised during harsh political times—WWI raged when she was a teenager—but was able to attend the affluent Maria Terezia Girls' School in Budapest, from where she graduated in one thousand nine hundred twenty two. She then studied at Pazmany Peter University (later renamed Lorand Eoetvoes University) in Budapest. She began studying chemistry at the insistence of her father, but later switched to mathematics, and graduated in one thousand nine hundred twenty seven. Although she had the credentials to teach high school mathematics, the economic situation at the time was dire as the Great Depression affected the world economy. During this time, Peter took odd jobs as a tutor and private teacher of mathematics. She eventually returned to university to take up graduate studies in mathematics. She had originally planned to work in number theory, but after finding out that her results had already been proven, she almost gave up on mathematics altogether. She was encouraged to work on Goedel's incompleteness theorems, and unknowingly proved several of his results in different ways. This restored her confidence, and Peter went on to write her first papers on recursion theory, inspired by David Hilbert's foundational program. She received her PhD in one thousand nine hundred thirty five, and in one thousand nine hundred thirty seven she became an editor for the Journal of Symbolic Logic. Peter's early papers are widely credited as founding contributions to the field of recursive function theory. In Rózsa Péter (one thousand nine hundred thirty fivea) , she investigated the relationship between different kinds of recursion. In Rózsa Péter (one thousand nine hundred thirty fiveb) , she showed that a certain recursively defined function is not primitive recursive. This simplified an earlier result due to Wilhelm Ackermann. Peter's simplified function is what's now often called the Ackermann function—and sometimes, more properly, the Ackermann—Peter function. She wrote the first book on recursive function theory (Rózsa Péter, one thousand nine hundred fifty one) . Despite the importance and influence of her work, Peter did not obtain a full-time teaching position until one thousand nine hundred forty five. During the Nazi occupation of Hungary during World War II, Peter was not allowed to teach due to anti-Semitic laws. In one thousand nine hundred forty four the government created a Jewish ghetto in Budapest; the ghetto was cut off from the rest of the city and attended by armed guards. Peter was forced to live in the ghetto until one thousand nine hundred forty five when it was liberated. She then went on to teach at the Budapest Teachers Training College, and from one thousand nine hundred fifty five onward at Eoetvoes Lorand University. She was the first female Hungarian mathematician to become an Academic Doctor of Mathematics, and the first woman to be elected to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. listen_text: Section. Julia Robinson. Julia Bowman Robinson was an American mathematician. She is known mainly for her work on decision problems, and most famously for her contributions to the solution of Hilbert's tenth problem. Robinson was born in St. Louis, Missouri, on December eight, one thousand nine hundred nineteen. Robinson recalls being intrigued by numbers already as a child (Constance Reid, one thousand nine hundred eighty six, four) . At age nine she contracted scarlet fever and suffered from several recurrent bouts of rheumatic fever. This forced her to spend much of her time in bed, putting her behind in her education. Although she was able to catch up with the help of private tutors, the physical effects of her illness had a lasting impact on her life. Despite her childhood struggles, Robinson graduated high school with several awards in mathematics and the sciences. She started her university career at San Diego State College, and transferred to the University of California, Berkeley, as a senior. There she was influenced by the mathematician Raphael Robinson. They became good friends, and married in one thousand nine hundred forty one. As a spouse of a faculty member, Robinson was barred from teaching in the mathematics department at Berkeley. Although she continued to audit mathematics classes, she hoped to leave university and start a family. Not long after her wedding, however, Robinson contracted pneumonia. She was told that there was substantial scar tissue build up on her heart due to the rheumatic fever she suffered as a child. Due to the severity of the scar tissue, the doctor predicted that she would not live past forty and she was advised not to have children (Constance Reid, one thousand nine hundred eighty six, thirteen) . Robinson was depressed for a long time, but eventually decided to continue studying mathematics. She returned to Berkeley and completed her PhD in one thousand nine hundred forty eight under the supervision of Alfred Tarski. The first-order theory of the real numbers had been shown to be decidable by Tarski, and from Goedel's work it followed that the first-order theory of the natural numbers is undecidable. It was a major open problem whether the first-order theory of the rationals is decidable or not. In her thesis (one thousand nine hundred forty nine) , Robinson proved that it was not. Interested in decision problems, Robinson next attempted to find a solution to Hilbert's tenth problem. This problem was one of a famous list of twenty three mathematical problems posed by David Hilbert in one thousand nine hundred. The tenth problem asks whether there is an algorithm that will answer, in a finite amount of time, whether or not a polynomial equation with integer coefficients, such as three x squared minus two y plus three equals zero , has a solution in the integers. Such questions are known as Diophantine problems. After some initial successes, Robinson joined forces with Martin Davis and Hilary Putnam, who were also working on the problem. They succeeded in showing that exponential Diophantine problems (where the unknowns may also appear as exponents) are undecidable, and showed that a certain conjecture (later called “J.R.”) implies that Hilbert's tenth problem is undecidable (Martin Davis and Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson, one thousand nine hundred sixty one) . Robinson continued to work on the problem throughout the nineteen sixties. In one thousand nine hundred seventy, the young Russian mathematician Yuri Matijasevich finally proved the J.R. hypothesis. The combined result is now called the Matijasevich—Robinson—Davis—Putnam theorem, or MRDP theorem for short. Matijasevich and Robinson became friends and collaborated on several papers. In a letter to Matijasevich, Robinson once wrote that “actually I am very pleased that working together (thousands of miles apart) we are obviously making more progress than either one of us could alone” (Yuri Matijasevich, one thousand nine hundred ninety two, forty five) . Robinson was the first female president of the American Mathematical Society, and the first woman to be elected to the National Academy of Science. She died on July thirty, one thousand nine hundred eighty five at the age of sixty five after being diagnosed with leukemia. Further reading. Robinson's mathematical papers are available in her Collected Works (Julia Robinson, one thousand nine hundred ninety six) , which also includes a reprint of her National Academy of Sciences biographical memoir (Solomon Feferman, one thousand nine hundred ninety four) . Robinson's older sister Constance Reid published an “Autobiography of Julia,” based on interviews (Constance Reid, one thousand nine hundred eighty six) , as well as a full memoir (Constance Reid, one thousand nine hundred ninety six) . A short documentary about Robinson and Hilbert's tenth problem was directed by George Csicsery (George Csicsery, two thousand sixteen) . For a brief memoir about Yuri Matijasevich's collaborations with Robinson, and her influence on his work, see (Yuri Matijasevich, one thousand nine hundred ninety two) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Bertrand Russell. Bertrand Russell is hailed as one of the founders of modern analytic philosophy. Born May eighteen, one thousand eight hundred seventy two, Russell was not only known for his work in philosophy and logic, but wrote many popular books in various subject areas. He was also an ardent political activist throughout his life. Russell was born in Trellech, Monmouthshire, Wales. His parents were members of the British nobility. They were free-thinkers, and even made friends with the radicals in Boston at the time. Unfortunately, Russell's parents died when he was young, and Russell was sent to live with his grandparents. There, he was given a religious upbringing (something his parents had wanted to avoid at all costs). His grandmother was very strict in all matters of morality. During adolescence he was mostly homeschooled by private tutors. Russell's influence in analytic philosophy, and especially logic, is tremendous. He studied mathematics and philosophy at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was influenced by the mathematician and philosopher Alfred North Whitehead. In one thousand nine hundred ten, Russell and Whitehead published the first volume of Principia Mathematica, where they championed the view that mathematics is reducible to logic. He went on to publish hundreds of books, essays and political pamphlets. In one thousand nine hundred fifty, he won the Nobel Prize for literature. Russell's was deeply entrenched in politics and social activism. During World War I he was arrested and sent to prison for six months due to pacifist activities and protest. While in prison, he was able to write and read, and claims to have found the experience “quite agreeable.” He remained a pacifist throughout his life, and was again incarcerated for attending a nuclear disarmament rally in one thousand nine hundred sixty one. He also survived a plane crash in one thousand nine hundred forty eight, where the only survivors were those sitting in the smoking section. As such, Russell claimed that he owed his life to smoking. Russell was married four times, but had a reputation for carrying on extra-marital affairs. He died on February two, one thousand nine hundred seventy at the age of ninety seven in Penrhyndeudraeth, Wales. Further reading. Russell wrote an autobiography in three parts, spanning his life from one thousand eight hundred seventy two to one thousand nine hundred sixty seven (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred sixty seven) and (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred sixty eight) and (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred sixty nine) . The Bertrand Russell Research Centre at McMaster University is home of the Bertrand Russell archives. See their website at Arlene Duncan (two thousand fifteen) , for information on the volumes of his collected works (including searchable indexes), and archival projects. Russell's paper On Denoting (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred five) is a classic of twentyth century analytic philosophy. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Russell (Andrew David Irvine, two thousand fifteen) has sound clips of Russell speaking on Desire and Political theory. Many video interviews with Russell are available online. To see him talk about smoking and being involved in a plane crash, for example, see Bertrand Russell (n.d.) . Some of Russell's works, including his Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy are available as free audiobooks on LibriVox (n.d.) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Alfred Tarski. Alfred Tarski was born on January fourteen, one thousand nine hundred one in Warsaw, Poland (then part of the Russian Empire). Described as “Napoleonic,” Tarski was boisterous, talkative, and intense. His energy was often reflected in his lectures—he once set fire to a wastebasket while disposing of a cigarette during a lecture, and was forbidden from lecturing in that building again. Tarski had a thirst for knowledge from a young age. Although later in life he would tell students that he studied logic because it was the only class in which he got a B, his high school records show that he got A's across the board—even in logic. He studied at the University of Warsaw from one thousand nine hundred eighteen to one thousand nine hundred twenty four. Tarski first intended to study biology, but became interested in mathematics, philosophy, and logic, as the university was the center of the Warsaw School of Logic and Philosophy. Tarski earned his doctorate in one thousand nine hundred twenty four under the supervision of Stanisław Lesniewski. Before emigrating to the United States in one thousand nine hundred thirty nine, Tarski completed some of his most important work while working as a secondary school teacher in Warsaw. His work on logical consequence and logical truth were written during this time. In one thousand nine hundred thirty nine, Tarski was visiting the United States for a lecture tour. During his visit, Germany invaded Poland, and because of his Jewish heritage, Tarski could not return. His wife and children remained in Poland until the end of the war, but were then able to emigrate to the United States as well. Tarski taught at Harvard, the College of the City of New York, and the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton, and finally the University of California, Berkeley. There he founded the multidisciplinary program in Logic and the Methodology of Science. Tarski died on October twenty six, one thousand nine hundred eighty three at the age of eighty two. Further reading. For more on Tarski's life, see the biography Alfred Tarski: Life and Logic (Anita Feferman and Solomon Feferman, two thousand four) . Tarski's seminal works on logical consequence and truth are available in English in (John Corcoran, one thousand nine hundred eighty three) . All of Tarski's original works have been collected into a four volume series, (Alfred Tarski, one thousand nine hundred eighty one) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Alan Turing. Alan Turing was born in Maida Vale, London, on June twenty three, one thousand nine hundred twelve. He is considered the father of theoretical computer science. Turing's interest in the physical sciences and mathematics started at a young age. However, as a boy his interests were not represented well in his schools, where emphasis was placed on literature and classics. Consequently, he did poorly in school and was reprimanded by many of his teachers. Turing attended King's College, Cambridge as an undergraduate, where he studied mathematics. In one thousand nine hundred thirty six Turing developed (what is now called) the Turing machine as an attempt to precisely define the notion of a computable function and to prove the undecidability of the decision problem. He was beaten to the result by Alonzo Church, who proved the result via his own lambda calculus. Turing's paper was still published with reference to Church's result. Church invited Turing to Princeton, where he spent one thousand nine hundred thirty six to one thousand nine hundred thirty eight, and obtained a doctorate under Church. Despite his interest in logic, Turing's earlier interests in physical sciences remained prevalent. His practical skills were put to work during his service with the British cryptanalytic department at Bletchley Park during World War II. Turing was a central figure in cracking the cypher used by German Naval communications—the Enigma code. Turing's expertise in statistics and cryptography, together with the introduction of electronic machinery, gave the team the ability to crack the code by creating a de-crypting machine called a “bombe.” His ideas also helped in the creation of the world's first programmable electronic computer, the Colossus, also used at Bletchley park to break the German Lorenz cypher. Turing was gay. Nevertheless, in one thousand nine hundred forty two he proposed to Joan Clarke, one of his teammates at Bletchley Park, but later broke off the engagement and confessed to her that he was homosexual. He had several lovers throughout his lifetime, although homosexual acts were then criminal offences in the UK. In one thousand nine hundred fifty two, Turing's house was burgled by a friend of his lover at the time, and when filing a police report, Turing admitted to having a homosexual relationship, under the impression that the government was on their way to legalizing homosexual acts. This was not true, and he was charged with gross indecency. Instead of going to prison, Turing opted for a hormone treatment that reduced libido. Turing was found dead on June eight, one thousand nine hundred fifty four, of a cyanide overdose—most likely suicide. He was given a royal pardon by Queen Elizabeth II in two thousand thirteen. Further reading. For a comprehensive biography of Alan Turing, see Andrew Hodges (two thousand fourteen) . Turing's life and work inspired a play, Breaking the Code, which was produced in one thousand nine hundred ninety six for TV starring Derek Jacobi as Turing. The Imitation Game, an Academy Award nominated film starring Bendict Cumberbatch and Kiera Knightley, is also loosely based on Alan Turing's life and time at Bletchley Park (Morten Tyldum, two thousand fourteen) . Radiolab (two thousand twelve) has several podcasts on Turing's life and work. BBC Horizon's documentary The Strange Life and Death of Dr. Turing is available to watch online (Christopher Sykes, one thousand nine hundred ninety two) . (Andre Theelen, two thousand twelve) is a short video of a working LEGO Turing Machine—made to honour Turing's centenary in two thousand twelve. Turing's original paper on Turing machines and the decision problem is Alan M. Turing (one thousand nine hundred thirty seven) . End further reading. End section.

listen_text: Section. Ernst Zermelo. Ernst Zermelo was born on July twenty seven, one thousand eight hundred seventy one in Berlin, Germany. He had five sisters, though his family suffered from poor health and only three survived to adulthood. His parents also passed away when he was young, leaving him and his siblings orphans when he was seventeen. Zermelo had a deep interest in the arts, and especially in poetry. He was known for being sharp, witty, and critical. His most celebrated mathematical achievements include the introduction of the axiom of choice (in one thousand nine hundred four), and his axiomatization of set theory (in one thousand nine hundred eight). Zermelo's interests at university were varied. He took courses in physics, mathematics, and philosophy. Under the supervision of Hermann Schwarz, Zermelo completed his dissertation Investigations in the Calculus of Variations in one thousand eight hundred ninety four at the University of Berlin. In one thousand eight hundred ninety seven, he decided to pursue more studies at the University of Goettigen, where he was heavily influenced by the foundational work of David Hilbert. In one thousand eight hundred ninety nine he became eligible for professorship, but did not get one until eleven years later—possibly due to his strange demeanour and “nervous haste.” Zermelo finally received a paid professorship at the University of Zurich in one thousand nine hundred ten, but was forced to retire in one thousand nine hundred sixteen due to tuberculosis. After his recovery, he was given an honourary professorship at the University of Freiburg in one thousand nine hundred twenty one. During this time he worked on foundational mathematics. He became irritated with the works of Thoralf Skolem and Kurt Goedel, and publicly criticized their approaches in his papers. He was dismissed from his position at Freiburg in one thousand nine hundred thirty five, due to his unpopularity and his opposition to Hitler's rise to power in Germany. The later years of Zermelo's life were marked by isolation. After his dismissal in one thousand nine hundred thirty five, he abandoned mathematics. He moved to the country where he lived modestly. He married in one thousand nine hundred forty four, and became completely dependent on his wife as he was going blind. Zermelo lost his sight completely by one thousand nine hundred fifty one. He passed away in Guenterstal, Germany, on May twenty one, one thousand nine hundred fifty three. Further reading. For a full biography of Zermelo, see Heinz-Dieter Ebbinghaus (two thousand fifteen) . Zermelo's seminal one thousand nine hundred four and one thousand nine hundred eight papers are available to read in the original German (Ernst Zermelo, one thousand nine hundred four) and (Ernst Zermelo, one thousand nine hundred eight) . Zermelo's collected works, including his writing on physics, are available in English translation in (Heinz-Dieter Ebbinghaus and Craig G. Fraser and Akihiro Kanamori, two thousand ten) and (Heinz-Dieter Ebbinghaus and Akihiro Kanamori, two thousand thirteen) . End further reading. End section. End chapter.

listen_text: Section. Infinitesimals and Differentiation. Newton and Leibniz discovered the calculus (independently) at the end of the seventeenth century. A particularly important application of the calculus was differentiation. Roughly speaking, differentiation aims to give a notion of the “rate of change”, or gradient, of a function at a point. Here is a vivid way to illustrate the idea. Consider the function f of x equals x squared over four plus one half , depicted in black below: Coordinate diagram for the function f of x equals x squared over four plus one half. The horizontal axis is x , and the vertical axis is f of x . The horizontal tick labels use the horizontal-axis tick values one through four ; the vertical tick labels use the vertical-axis tick values one through five . A black upward-opening parabola is shown. Three right secant triangles share the point where x is one half. The red triangle has base three and slope one; the smaller blue triangle has base two and slope three quarters; the smallest green triangle has base one and slope one half. End diagram. Suppose we want to find the gradient of the function at c equals one half . We start by drawing a triangle whose hypotenuse approximates the gradient at that point, perhaps the red triangle above. When beta is the base length of our triangle, its height is f of one half plus beta, minus f of one half , so that the gradient of the hypotenuse is: Displayed expression. the quantity f of one half plus beta, minus f of one half, divided by beta. End displayed expression. So the gradient of our red triangle, with base length three , is exactly one . The hypotenuse of a smaller triangle, the blue triangle with base length two , gives a better approximation; its gradient is three quarters . A yet smaller triangle, the green triangle with base length one , gives a yet better approximation; with gradient one half . Ever-smaller triangles give us ever-better approximations. So we might say something like this: the hypotenuse of a triangle with an infinitesimal base length gives us the gradient at c equals one half itself. In this way, we would obtain a formula for the (first) derivative of the function f at the point c : Displayed expression. f prime of c equals the quantity f of c plus beta minus f of c, divided by beta, where beta is infinitesimal. End displayed expression. And, roughly, this is what Newton and Leibniz said. However, since they have said this, we must ask them: what is an infinitesimal? A serious dilemma arises. If beta equals zero , then f prime is ill-defined, for it involves dividing by zero . But if beta is greater than zero , then we just get an approximation to the gradient, and not the gradient itself. This is not an anachronistic concern. Here is Berkeley, criticizing Newton's followers: Quotation. I admit that signs may be made to denote either any thing or nothing: and consequently that in the original notation c plus beta , beta might have signified either an increment or nothing. But then which of these soever you make it signify, you must argue consistently with such its signification, and not proceed upon a double meaning: Which to do were a manifest sophism. ( George Berkeley one thousand seven hundred thirty four, section thirteen , variables changed to match preceding text) End quotation. To defend the infinitesimal calculus against Berkeley, one might reply that the talk of “infinitesimals” is merely figurative. One might say that, so long as we take a really small triangle, we will get a good enough approximation to the tangent. Berkeley had a reply to this too: whilst that might be good enough for engineering, it undermines the status of mathematics, for Quotation. we are told that in rebus mathematicis errores quam minimi non sunt contemnendi. Translation. In the case of mathematics, the smallest errors are not to be neglected. End translation. (George Berkeley, one thousand seven hundred thirty four, section nine) End quotation. The italicised passage is a near-verbatim quote from Newton's own Quadrature of Curves (one thousand seven hundred four). Berkeley's philosophical objections are deeply incisive. Nevertheless, the calculus was a massively successful enterprise, and mathematicians continued to use it without falling into error. End section.

listen_text: Section. Pathologies. However, the definition of a limit turned out to allow for some rather “pathological” constructions. Around the eighteen thirties, Bolzano discovered a function which was continuous everywhere, but differentiable nowhere. (Unfortunately, Bolzano never published this; the idea was first encountered by mathematicians in one thousand eight hundred seventy two, thanks to Weierstrass's independent discovery of the same idea.) Footnote. The history is documented in extremely thorough footnotes to the Wikipedia article on the linked Wikipedia article on the Weierstrass function . End footnote. This was, to say the least, rather surprising. It is easy to find functions, such as the absolute value of x , which are continuous everywhere but not differentiable at a particular point. But a function which is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere is a very different beast. Consider, for a moment, how you might try to draw such a function. To ensure it is continuous, you must be able to draw it without ever removing your pen from the page; but to ensure it is differentiable nowhere, you would have to abruptly change the direction of your pen, constantly. Further “pathologies” followed. In January five one thousand eight hundred seventy four, Cantor wrote a letter to Dedekind, posing the problem: Quotation. Can a surface (say a square including its boundary) be one-to-one correlated to a line (say a straight line including its endpoints) so that to every point of the surface there corresponds a point of the line, and conversely to every point of the line there corresponds a point of the surface? It still seems to me at the moment that the answer to this question is very difficult—although here too one is so impelled to say no that one would like to hold the proof to be almost superfluous. Attribution. Quoted in Fernando Q. Gouvêa two thousand eleven . End attribution. End quotation. But, in one thousand eight hundred seventy seven, Cantor proved that he had been wrong. In fact, a line and a square have exactly the same number of points. He wrote on twenty nine June one thousand eight hundred seventy seven to Dedekind “ je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas ”; that is, “I see it, but I don't believe it”. In the “received history” of mathematics, this is often taken to indicate just how literally incredible these new results were to the mathematicians of the time. (The correspondence is presented in Fernando Q. Gouvêa (two thousand eleven) , and we return to it in the section More Myth than History . Cantor's proof is outlined in the section Cantor on the Line and the Plane .) Inspired by Cantor's result, Peano started to consider whether it might be possible to map a line smoothly onto a plane. This would be a curve which fills space. In one thousand eight hundred ninety , Peano constructed just such a curve. This is truly counter-intuitive: Euclid had defined a line as “breadthless length” (Book I, Definition two), but Peano had shown that, by curling up a line appropriately, its length can be turned into breadth. In one thousand eight hundred ninety one , Hilbert described a slightly more intuitive space-filling curve, together with some pictures illustrating it. The curve is constructed in sequence, and here are the first six stages of the construction: Six square panels show the first six Hilbert-curve approximations in source order: stages one, two, and three across the top row, then stages four, five, and six across the bottom row. Each red curve lies in a gray square. The step sizes halve from stage to stage, while the recursive order rises from one through six, making the curve increasingly dense. No arrow direction, coordinate label, or filled region is printed. End diagram. In the limit—a notion which had, by now, received rigorous definition—the entire square is filled in solid red. And, in passing, Hilbert's curve is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere; intuitively because, in the infinite limit, the function abruptly changes direction at every moment. (We will outline Hilbert's construction in more detail in the appendix on Hilbert's space-filling curves .) For better or worse, these “pathological” geometric constructions were treated as a reason to doubt appeals to geometric intuition. They became something approaching propaganda for a new way of doing mathematics, which would culminate in set theory. In the later myth-building of the subject, it was repeated, often, that these results were both perfectly rigorous and perfectly shocking. They therefore served a dual purpose: as a warning against relying upon geometric intuition, and as a demonstration of the fertility of new ways of thinking. End section.

listen_text: Section. More Myth than History?. Looking back on these events with more than a century of hindsight, we must be careful not to take these verdicts on trust. The results were certainly novel, exciting, and surprising. But how truly shocking were they? And did they really demonstrate that we should not rely on geometric intuition? On the question of shock, Fernando Q. Gouvêa (two thousand eleven) points out that Cantor's famous note to Dedekind, “ je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas ” is taken rather out of context. Here is more of that context (quoted from Fernando Q. Gouvêa ): Quotation. Please excuse my zeal for the subject if I make so many demands upon your kindness and patience; the communications which I lately sent you are even for me so unexpected, so new, that I can have no peace of mind until I obtain from you, honoured friend, a decision about their correctness. So long as you have not agreed with me, I can only say: je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas. End quotation. Cantor knew his result was “so unexpected, so new”. But it is doubtful that he ever found his result unbelievable. As Fernando Q. Gouvêa points out, he was simply asking Dedekind to check the proof he had offered. On the question of geometric intuition: Peano published his space-filling curve without including any diagrams. But when Hilbert published his curve, he explained his purpose: he would provide readers with a clear way to understand Peano's result, if they “help themselves to the following geometric intuition”; whereupon he included a series of diagrams just like those provided in the section Pathologies . More generally: whilst diagrams have fallen rather out of fashion in published proofs, there is no getting round the fact that mathematicians frequently use diagrams when proving things. (Roughly put: good mathematicians know when they can rely upon geometric intuition.) In short: don't believe the hype; or at least, don't just take it on trust. For more on this, you could read Marcus Giaquinto (two thousand seven) . End section.

listen_text: Section. Appendix: Hilbert's Space-filling Curves. In chapter the section Pathologies , we mentioned that Cantor's proof that a line and a square have exactly the same number of points ( the theorem that the unit interval and unit square have equal cardinality ) prompted Peano to ask whether there might be a space-filling curve. He obtained a positive answer in one thousand eight hundred ninety. In this section, we explain (in a hand-wavy way) how to construct Hilbert's space-filling curve (with a tiny tweak). Footnote. For a more rigorous explanation, see Nicholas J Rose (two thousand ten) . The tweak amounts to the inclusion of the red parts of the curves below. This makes it slightly easier to check that the curve is continuous. End footnote. We must define a function, h , as the limit of a sequence of functions h sub one , h sub two , h sub three , and so on We first describe the construction. Then we show it is space-filling. Then we show it is a curve. We will take h apostrophe s range to be the unit square, the unit square . Here is our first approximation to h , that is, h sub one : First Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by a two by two grid. A black first-order Hilbert path connects the four quarter-cells in the order bottom left, top left, top right, bottom right. Short red segments connect the two bottom endpoints to the square boundary. End diagram. To keep track of things, we have imposed a two by two grid on the square. We can think of the curve starting in the bottom left quarter, moving to the top left, then to the top right, then finally to the bottom right. Here is the second stage in the construction, that is, h sub two : Second Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by a four by four grid. Four scaled black copies of the first-order core occupy the quarter-squares. The lower-left copy is rotated two hundred seventy degrees, the two upper copies are unrotated, and the lower-right copy is rotated ninety degrees. Three green segments join consecutive copies, and two red segments connect the outer endpoints to the left and right boundary. End diagram. The different colours will help explain how h sub two was constructed. We first place scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub one into the bottom left, top left, top right, and bottom right of our square (drawn in black). We then connect these four figures (with green lines). Finally, we connect our figure to the boundary of the square (with red lines). Now to h sub three . Just as h sub two was made from four connected, scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub one , so h sub three is made up of four scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub two (drawn in black), which are then joined together (with green lines) and finally connected to the boundary of the square (with red lines). Third Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by an eight by eight grid. Four scaled black copies of the second-order core occupy the quarter-squares. The lower-left copy is rotated two hundred seventy degrees, the two upper copies are unrotated, and the lower-right copy is rotated ninety degrees. The source draws three distinct green connector positions, but repeats the right connector command once at the same coordinates; two red segments connect the outer endpoints to the bottom boundary. End diagram. And now we see the general pattern for defining h sub n plus one from h sub n . At last we define the curve h itself by considering the point-by-point limit of these successive functions h sub one , h sub two , and so on That is, for each x is a point of the unit square : Displayed expression. h of x equals the limit, as n tends to infinity, of h sub n of x. End displayed expression. We now show that this curve fills space. When we draw the curve h sub n , we impose a two to the n by two to the n grid onto the unit square . By Pythagoras's Theorem, the diagonal of each grid-location is of length: Displayed expression. the square root of the sum of two copies of one over two to the n, squared, equals two to the power one half minus n.
